This is a neat little game with some very big frustration.  The premise is simple, you command the crew of a small starship who must escape from an ever advancing enemy armada in a desperate attempt to reach safety with your own fleet. Along the way you'll find yourself fighting other ships in individual combat and engaging in random events whose outcomes are decided primarily on random chance, crew selection, and equipment selection.  As you jump into each new sector, the difficulty will ramp up considerably, meaning if you are unlucky or adopt poor tactics, you will quickly die. This can and usually does result in frustration and may put some off from playing the game. Keep in mind there are no retries in this game, so each death means you start over from scratch.  If you like a very challenging strategy game, you might try this, but dont expect any huge fleet type battles. This is strictly a one on one fight kind of game.

Writing a positive review for the following reasons:  -It's actually a good game, arguably the most fun co-op shooter there is. It looks great, runs great and plays great. Not much developers can nail the satisfying feel of emptying a gun into your enemies as Tripwire can. It's a hordemode shooter where you are surviving against waves of enemies of increasing difficulty with tons of gore (some of the best gore in games at the time of release/reviewing this).  If you expect a deep story or the next competitive big thing look elsewhere, this is not the game for that - know what you buy before you purchase.  -To offset the negativity surrounding the announced 'microtransactions' about cosmetic weapon skins. As usual something like this is bound to cause a kneejerk shitstorm of every aspiring redditor that feels he is the voice of reason the world needs (instead of in reality, being the next incessant whiner in line). Newsflash, this is nothing new - games with a similar pricing such as CS:GO or DOTA 2/Team Fortress (when they were B2P) have the exact same model and are highly succesful. Because it's Valve however, it seems to be magically excused - hypocrisy at it's finest. Not to mention the business model also benefits content creators aside from the developer.  Let's be honest here, in no way am I trying to be apologetic for microtransactions as I am far from a fan of this practice, but the fact remains: as long as this has no impact on the gameplay then there is nothing wrong with this model if it can help in the development of further content. People seem to have forgotten that in KF1 the skin packs that were sold led to the creation of tons of free content updates like the multiple christmas, summer & easter content releases - or do you believe content like that requires no manpower and loads of work hours?  This metabombing is absolutely ridiculous, then again - who really takes user reviews serious these days?  People with over 60-100 hours of gametime (which somehow obviously means they enjoy the game, right?) are now posting a negative review out of spite or feeling edgy by joining the hate bandwagon, classic stuff.  $25 for over 100 hours of entertainment, pretty good damn value to me but go ahead and enjoy hating on anything you can.  Next up on the news: Whine about buying an EA game because it has EA content and isn't finished, game development should take less than 6 months to create a fully fleshed out game.  -------------------------------------  Edit response to pcsoldier:  Honestly I shouldn't bother answering because we aren't going to convince one another to change our opinions, let alone have a decent discussion on the Steam boards.  All I will add is that developing videogames consists of multiple teams with programmers of all types of 'specialization' (eg. UI, gameplay, engine, etc) that all have their task to fullfill.  'Content' like this doesn't require a whole lot of persons to implement, potentially only a couple of people can get a feature like this up & running. This can easily be made by even interns, people that wouldn't even be part of the main group of programmers at all. Though I don't know how TWI works on the inside, I can pretty confidentially say this implementation wouldn't take away from developing the core of the game (eg. finishing the early access and launch the title fully featured).  People have absolutely no idea what kind of work hours it takes to create a quality game like this -not to mention have it largely bug-free-, let alone the costs of running a 50+ members team to sustain itself each month. I do not endorse mictrotransactions at all but in all honesty it can be a necessary evil, creating games costs tons and tons of money if you want to join in on the (semi-)cutting edge level.  This game delivers AAA quality in terms of production value and $25 per sale (standard sale) isn't going to cut it to keep your head afloat in the long run for a company. And it will NOT cut it at all to deliver free content in the form of maps, weapons, enemies on the longterm, which is what the exact reason something like this is being implemented.  After all, KF1 had packs they sold aswell and people that never bought a single one of them benefited from people that did buy them since they funded free content like the christmas or summer or weapon updates, etc.  What is essentially free content for a large part of the playerbase is basically being funded by the people that willingly buy DLC, this is nothing new mind you, funds do not magically appear out of thin air to pay for manpower & work hours.  If you want TWI to stay afloat and keep making games you enjoy then you will deal with the fact that MT's help alleviate the pressure to gain a certain amount of monthly income. If these MT's are not of the pay2win sort I can completely live with them even though I certainly am not a fan - infact I hate what TF2 has become and I paid €60 back in the day for it. But TWI is not a comparable developer to Valve at all when it comes down to income or profit and I can understand they could probably make good use of MT's like this to earn some money for further content contrary to Valve which doesn't need it at all yet still threw it in CS GO.  Arguements about 'they are slow in delivering content' is frankly a load of bull, basically pure hyperboling. If you hate it so much to wait for 'content' which is basically implementing a fully featured game, then you should not buy into an EA title and wait for the full launch - it really is that simple since nobody is forcing you to buy the title.  People that demand refunds while playing over 100 hours or cracking down on TWI are quite simply put, completely delusional and have some kind of botched-up sense of overentitlement and are largely uninformed in the matter.  Maybe one day when some people have grown out of adolescence they might see their folly in stirring up a shitstorm over something as trivial as this and realize why things like cosmetic MT's get implemented in the evergrowing costly dev business. Nothing in the world comes for free and game development is a dog-eat-dog business.

The keyboard control handling is not designed well at all.  Mouse input is not enabled so all of the input must be handled via the keyboard if you do not have a controller/gamepad.  The primary reason why keyboard input is designed poorly which significantly affects the gameplay is using the special combo (its called RS in this game).  Using RS is awkward because either you can use a meta key (shift) plus the direction to boost up/down/left/right (with the default shell) or bind your own keyboard shortcut for each RS direction (up/down/left/right).  This boost requires the opposite direction press.  For instance, if you want to boost forward, you need to hit meta + back arrow.  Its not intuitive and makes controlling the default shell unnecessarily difficult.  It would be so much easier if they implemented mouse control where the boost would go in the direction of where the mouse is pointing.    Input handling for the default shell in my opinion is broken or at the very least horribly designed.  The default shell has the artificial limitation of not being able to move and shoot at the same time unless the shell is in the air.  This limitation does not make any sense and I never played a 2d side scroller that had this requirement.  Imagine playing Contra or any 2d side scroller with this limitation.  Its simply not fun.  And anyone saying 'git good' simply hasn't been alive long enough to understand that the mechanics for 2d side scrollers are well established and adding this limitation does not make sense.  I have heard some say that the default shell would be over powered if they allowed running and shooting.  I say, the rest of their game design is broken if they needed to add this limitation in order to balance the shells.  Running and shooting in a 2d side scroller should be a given.  The developer IS NOT doing anything innovative by adding this limitation and I really do not think anyone needs to 'git good' using such an impractical mechanic.  My advice to the developer is to balance their game within the context of a 2d side scroller.  Allow running and shooting.  Since this game is on Steam, the majority of steam users USE keyboard and mouse input.  Implement mouse aim.  If you do these things, I will change my review as I think the game has potential.   As for now, I simply cannot recommend this title due to the input handling as I think its overall a frustrating experience.

Frostpunk combines a small scale SimCity, a decent story weaved through it, and the everything is terrible and all your choices are terrible of This War is Mine. This seems an unlikely combination of genres, yet I found that the end result was very enjoyable and would recommend it.  The game can be difficult, especially before you understand all the systems in place. But if you can manage to get your economic engine going, you can outpace the encroaching cold, even on hard mode.   The first few playthroughs, when the mystery and terribleness of your choices are driving you onward are compelling to the experience of the game. And even when you view the decisions you make in purely mechanical terms, the choices you make always feel like they have some ramification down the line.  I will also say that of the three base scenarios in the game, I enjoyed the Arks scenario the most. So just because you beat A New Home, you are not done with the game just yet.

I might add from the start that I bought this game through the Microsoft Store when the game was released so my total playtime is much higher.  How to start? Well this is a game with a bit of a troubled launch to say the least. While a functional game it was really barebones. A big world with nothing really in it besides the same 3 missions over and over again. But how is the game now at it's Steam release? Well it is in a much better state without a doubt. From skeleton ships that can show up and mess with you to a bigger map with more natural hazards. Add to this with 1 more faction added that you can earn reputation for to more weapons and items, quests and a new ship. So there is more to do with still with room to expand even further.  Graphics are still top-notch with it's stylized look in their characters giving it it's own rather unique look to the gorgeous scenery and water with great sounds to accompany it.  Sailing which will take up most of your playtime isn't hardcore or complex but it isn't totally shallow either. You need to keep a watch on the wind and raise and lower the sail(sails depending on ship) and angle them as well in order to get the most out of the wind. And yet the sailing is easily the most enjoyable aspect of the game with the ships behaving well with the water and waves rocking the boat in a realistic manner. Getting caught in a storm can be quite a challenge just trying to keep a steady course and preventing the ship from getting flooded. Beware if you got a weak stomach since sea sickness is a possiblity.  Combat is as basic as it gets but it works. Same with enemies where you are either fighting skeletons, snakes or other players. But there is some variation when it comes to the skeletons like with some golden skeletons being very hard to kill to shadow skeletons that can only be hurt when in the light.  Naturally the game isn't perfect(few are). Main being is that it might not be totally fun if you are a solo player. With 3 ships available, there is really only 1 ship for solo players since the other 2 ships are too big to be handled by 1 person. And it's always more fun to play with others. Thankfully there is a matchmaking service so anyone sailing with a open crew slot you can join in.  Expansions are released free of charge and the game has microtransactions but it's for cosmetics only and most cosmetics you can unlock by simply playing the game.  Overall I recommend this game.

Appoint your companions to advisor positions, letting them attend to kingdom-related events and projects for you. Neat. But the way it was implemented, with next to zero documentation and meager/useless tutorial messages, means that several weeks into playing the game, my game abruptly ENDED with some kingdom failure message. Game Over. Apparently, my kingdom's Stability stat hit zero because I failed to resolve some event, I think? I'm still not clear on what the hell even happened. Great design, right? Luckily, or so I thought, the game then gave me an option to load a previous save with an option to prevent kingdom stats/events/projects from ending the game. Swell, but now another week in and nearly all of my advisors have a 0% chance to succeed at any event/project. I'll be damned if I'm starting the grind of this game all over again just to panic/flail wildly at the kingdom screen. Maybe I'll google a 3rd party tutorial on the kingdom stuff at some point in the future, but for now? Uninstall, game uncompleted.

[i][h1][b][u]I can't recall having played, if ever, a fantasy RPG game quite as enjoyable and engaging as The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt.[/u][/b][/h1][/i]  It would be an understatement to say that this game is my favorite game of the year. It's quite possibly my favorite fantasy RPG game of the last decade. I've played tons of fantasy RPG games from Diablo, the Elder Scrolls series, the Dragon Age series, and so much more... The Witcher 3 gives me everything I ever loved from those games and then some. It throws me in a world that seems more real then the rest, but yet so surreal at the same time that it remains completely fascinating. One of the truely special things about the Witcher games is that nothing is ever so black and white. Characters in that game feel so much more relatable and down to earth. It's never as simple as good and evil. Nothing is super obvious and you really have to think about your decisions. There are long term consequences to your actions and I was really surprised to see some of my choices I made early in the game come back and bite me in the ass later on. It's not all bad, but boy do I have some regrets and I love that it makes me feel that way.  I enjoyed the main story throughout the game and even more so that some of the side quests seemed to tie into the main storyline in very interesting ways. Speaking of the side quests, I can't get enough of em'. They are so well designed and well written. Every side quest has a purpose, every single one. There are big choices to be made in side quests, and their consequences. There are no filler quests or time wasters like a certain other game I played last year... AHEM AKUAHA * DRAGON AGE * Aghkgh .. .eh.. ah.. Yeah, Dragon Age Inquisition. Side quests in that game bored me to death. But not Witcher 3. Oh no. I enjoyed my journey all the way to the bitter end.  I want more! I do. Even after 185 hours, i'm still craving more Witcher 3. I don't usually start a second playthrough so soon after finishing the first, but boom there it is. If an awesome story and sidequests weren't enough I also found the combat to be super visceral and engaging. They've made huge strides and improvements since Witcher 2 and every movement and swing of the sword is very fluid and the animations for Geralt are something to behold. On that note lets also talk about the graphics. I believe Witcher 3 is the best looking game i've ever played on PC to date. I know the graphics were toned down a little and aren't exactly what they showed at E3, but it's still the best looking game around.. probably even better looking with the mods that are sure to come. Besides i'm pretty sure it wouldn't run all that great for most people if they didn't tone it down a notch. It's not all that bad, stop your whining kids. They did what they had to do to make it functional. I'm glad they did, honestly. It looks glorious at the highest settings and i'm getting a good enough framerate. Hops between 48 and 60 fps since I have Nvidia hairworks enabled.. which I personally thought looked pretty cool. If you can have that enabled and maintain a decent framerate I recommend keeping it on.  There's about a million great things I can say about The Witcher 3, and all the negative things about it were already fixed in patches, or are being fixed in future patches. The developers show their love to the game and their fans by keeping ontop of things and not only that, but they've been releasing free top quality DLC periodically. I'm talking full fledged quests, fully voice acted with choices and consequences of their own. New outfits for you and your horse. New outfits for other characters. Some more cosmetic stuff, and nice little additions. But those free quests man, damn that's awesome. Anyway, here's hoping that other companies and developers take a couple pages out of CD Projekt Red's book. More games of this caliber would be most welcome, especially if their aimed towards the PC community first and foremost as they should be.  So do I recommend this game? Mhm. Without a doubt.  Final Verdict: (5 out of 5)

I had been wanting to get to Ronin for a while though, I was pretty excited about it. After beating Gunpoint and I saw this one, it’s a slightly turn based version of Gunpoint, very similar anyway, except even in the hints in the game itself it says “this is not Gunpoint” haha. But the similarities are Very high. Graphics are very similar, level design is extremely similar, gameplay is quite similar. I don’t remember Gunpoints soundtrack, but the Ronin soundtrack is pretty good.  First, the bad, the really really bad, stupid idiotically bad. You can’t play this game in anything other than 1920x1080 resolution. [I don’t know if smaller works or not, I’d wager it does not]. My screen is 2560x1440. The options only allows a checkmark for full screen or not full screen. Obviously I play full screen, but when I got to a point where I had to kill a guard, a little red sword button pops up. Except I couldn’t click it. Somehow I did it accidentally. I pressed every key on the kb and nothing worked. I couldn’t progress. I looked for a manual or guide as to what button to push. I almost quit the game outright, never to be played again. Then I found a steam forum post about the resolution issue. Unchecked fullscreen, which puts it to 1920x1080 and it has worked flawlessly ever since.  So, once I was able to actually play, you jump around like gunpoint, you hack terminals by pressing up like gunpoint, you avoid and attack guards like gunpoint, you hide in shadows like gunpoint. It’s so ridiculously similar to gunpoint, EXCEPT, it’s semi-turn based, in a weird kinda way. Every second of time equates a movement, or something. It’s hard to explain. The game is real time until action starts and It auto-pauses. You can choose to jump (and choose your arc, which apparently is occasionally a lie) and sometimes your jump would last longer than a full turn, so you would land on the second turn (or do something else), you can attack, you can use grappling line, or another special unlocked ability. If you choose to attack while in a red line of death (enemy gun aim or whatever) then you would do your attack and then be shot. Unless your attack moves you, which it seems to do randomly – this is bad because it’s not always entirely predictable, though it usually is. So, you do a whole lot of jumping around until you get a clear attack of opportunity.   Which brings me to the next point, the difficulty spike is pretty intense. This game is HARD. There are, idk 7 bosses I think, and each one has a couple preliminary missions where you hack terminals. There really doesn’t seem to be much of a story. Gunpoint at least had an ok story mixed with some humor. But I haven’t even gotten to boss #2 yet. I have died SO MANY times. I enjoyed playing but I eventually got fatigued and went on to play some [semi]brainless OW. It’s almost like a puzzle game or a test of patience. So, if you can’t do that, then I don’t recommend it. Taylor, since you liked Dark Souls so much, you might like it, especially since you liked Gunpoint. Gunpoint is a piece of cake in comparison.  Combat tends to be in a room with 3-4 enemies. There are basic guards, who stay in one spot and shoot at your last location. Samurai that do a slash-n-dash in a straight trajectory, soldiers that seem to basically be the same as guards but have machine guns (I really don’t know the difference yet – apparently guards shoot second, soldiers shoot first), and some guys that are more prone to call for lockdown. [more on this in a minute] I think later on there are a couple more types. Guards, soldiers, and whatever the other guy is called can be knocked down and it takes two turns for them to get back up. You can kill them after knocking them down. Samurai are the most troublesome. You can’t jump at them, they take two hits to kill and you can only hit them in certain circumstances it seems. One hit stuns them, next hit kills. And of course they are dashing all over the room. Occasionally you can knock someone off a high ledge to kill them, but it doesn’t happen often.  The lockdown – locks certain doors impeding travel, calls more guards (I think), and more importantly fails one of your objectives. There are three objectives (usually) to each mission. If you complete them all, you get a skill point. If you don’t you can move on, but no point. Skill points give you things like the ability to throw a sword, throw shurikens to stun, have a body double, silently hang people from the ceiling, etc etc.   So, ultimately, it’s a really neat, cool game with some problems, but I really enjoyed it so far. I’ll definitely be playing again when I can devote the brain power.

As Paradox DLC's go, this one has a decent amount of content. For that alone, I'm recommending it.   But the balancing leaves something to be desired, even after a patch or two.  All of the mega-structures, with the exception of the Habitat, generally appear too late to be all that meaningful, and the only way to rush to them is via, uh, culture. Yeah, culture. A sci-fi game has, for reasons I can't begin to imagine, made the most epic structures into something that requires the new Ascension perk system, which is all about culture.   It's like if you wanted to build a nuke in Civ 6 but had to unlock a particular government to do so, or wanted to get the best equipment in Hearts of Iron IV but had to unlock 60 focuses first. It makes no sense whatsoever.   Further, it's a decent amount of content, but for 19.99 it's probably a tad on the shallow side... 19.99 is a third of the cost of the base game. Now, compared to the Eu-IV 'expansions', it actually stacks up pretty well. But as long as the balance is so wonky, you either need to rush culture, or play with mods, should you want to actually use much of anything other than the Habitat when it comes to those neat-o structures.   Marginal recommendation... on sale, even at $15.00, I'd say to scoop it up without a second though, but at $20.00, it could stand to have a little more to it.

I really wanted to like this game. The art, animation, and music are stunning, and its an interesting premise. Unfortunately, none of the parts work particularly well, and the overall experience falls flat.  AoG is essentially a visual novel with turn based combat. You travel between locations and have a few limited interactions at each. The first problem is the writing; its awkward, stilted, and hard to follow, which is a pain because theres a ton of dialogue and its a central feature of the game. The text is important too, as there are a lot of important decisions to be made, but I always felt like there was no way to predict the outcome from my choice. I was essentially making important decisions at random. Theres a resource management element of the game tied to the dialogue choices, and I felt like a wrong choice could leave me in a dead state down the road, but with no way to tell except from slogging through hours of gameplay and hoping you made the right call. I like the idea of choices and consequences, and not save-scumming for the optimal outcome, but the implementation is just too vague.  I'd ignore all of that if the combat was good, but unfortunately its lacking as well. Theres very little in the way of character customization, party choice, abilities, equipment, and even tactics. I wasn't expecting something as complex as Divinity: Original Sin, but you can still have some complexity with a fairly basic system.  Overall, theres some good ideas, but they just dont come together in an enjoyable way.

As a walking simulator, The Park is by far not the greatest but equally far from being the worst. Taking place in an abandoned amusement park very shortly after beginning, most of the game you'll spend on your own, wandering around Atlantic Island Park, looking for your son Callum. There, you'll travel through numerous rides and areas to the final destination within, wherein you discover the truth about why you're there.  Walking simulators, by their nature, often live and die on their writing, characters and world-building. What I will say I like the most about The Park is its sense of place. I love the amusement park setting, especially the idea of exploring it at night. It's something I enjoy a lot in real-life, when I can ride Splash Mountain late in the evening at Tokyo Disney. And whilst there's a few cool details: a rollercoaster, a dark ride, a house of horrors (amongst others), the environment surrounding these setpieces is sadly lacking. What should be a sprawling park is actually a circular pathway. A lot of these details, bar a few, can be simply ignored completely in order to progress the narrative. There's a lack of encouragement to explore, by virtue of how linear the world is. However, the first impression is nice, if only for the one time you experience it.  The narrative, however, is a different story. Right from the get-go, the game drops you into the spooky setting instead of allowing a slowburn introduction. I can see their intent to emulate a psychological state/dream/emotional collapse, but it's so sudden that the character investment and exposition is dragged behind the player. It's a shame because it actually stilts the player's perspective quite strongly. It's as if a horror film opens with the killer having cut the power to the remote house instead of giving me a proper sense of characters at risk, their lives, who they are and what's going on.  But then the themes make this even more problematic. Funcom writers are obviously no stranger to thematic resonance in their worlds, so 10 minutes in you get told a popular fairytale via a ride. However, these goes on for five to ten minutes in-and-of itself. Having just thrown you into the spookiness, the game bizarrely slows down to beat you over the head with one of the game's central themes with painfully obvious foreshadowing. It's really quite ridiculous and it keeps coming up later on, however from a worse source: the character's internal monologue. Unfortunately, the deep, lurid psychological tapestry of the protagonist that the game wants to build is a bit of a jambled mess up until the last 10 minutes, which takes the form of a blatant rip from P.T - the cancelled Kojima/Del Toro Silent Hills project. Still, this is arguably the strongest part of the game. The story is full of suggestions of an external force of fear/death, even putting the park mascot Chad on most of the game's advertising. However, he seldom even appears as a threat. Only once in the entire game did he actually become a frightening figure. When the inner psychological torment is personified, he appears more as a cartoonish character than a deep, trauma-driven force.  The end result is a game that, whilst I think it has a lot of promise in its beginning and I admire its initial storytelling approach and story world, is ultimately a poorly judged narrative. There's a great deal of exposition and it ultimately clogs the already stilted ability for the player to invest in the character. The themes are very clumsily handled instead of being the slow, subtle burn it should have been, giving both the world and player more identity by making the environment more than a series of setpieces. The world feels empty, both in a good and bad way. With more time and focused expression, I'm sure that world and story could have worked more cohesively together. But that's unfortunately not the case. Aesthetically, it's a nice experience and worth playing, if only for that.  The Park is a slow, singular decline into insanity that doesn't hit the marks it wants to. But, it's worth playing once, even if just to experience that attempt to hit the targets it's very clearly aspiring to hit.   TL;DR - It's not great but worth playing once. Buy on sale or in a bundle only.

I was looking forward to this after being kinda concerned it would never be, and based on my enjoyment of the first part, this one did not disappoint. Classic point and click adventure with the worst possible part being a puzzle or two that can be a bit difficult to figure out exactly what the game wants you to do. I had heard of some possible buggy parts, but did not encounter any on my playthrough so I can't say for certain what the deal is behind those.  Definitely a high point is the richness of the setting while simultaneously not requiring you to know the super dense lore from Homestuck to get into. The bite sized approach is as appreciated this time as it was last time. Characters are generally quirky, fun, well designed, and generally memorable. That even random background characters have unique designs is an especially nice touch.  On the downside, I do feel that [spoiler]the trial sequence dragged on quite a bit and could be frequently unintuitive to solve all for an overly long Phoenix Wright parody. I feel that section was disproportionately lengthy compared to the other sections and not quite as entertaining due to the gameplay deviation, though admittedly, I've always found trial sequences in video games rather tedious.[/spoiler] It did create a feeling that the other sections might be underdeveloped or rushed in comparison, though I did still enjoy them.  Also, the choice in music track for one particular section [spoiler]the gold/olive car[/spoiler] had a classic 8 bit sound that got kinda annoying to hear on loop given how long I spent in that particular area.  I do hope Hiveswap is able to fully complete it's story and while I understand that game development is a complicated matter, it would be nice to not have to wait several more years for parts 3 and 4 given how relatively short these are.

Arcade tactical combat at it's finest. Surprisingly good for a mobile port to the PC, the gameplay is good for what it is and the graphics are stylized and work well.  Combat appears simple, though it requires thought and strategy. Sometimes taking cover and shooting works well, other times running and gunning (with rolling and dodging) is best. It all depends on what's shooting or throwing grenades at you, or self destructs (scary). Different weapons (and armor) for different situations, which are unlocked for purchase by meeting various criteria. You can carry up to two weapons at once and switch on the fly. Various upgrades are also available for purchase once sufficient funds and upgrade chips are collected.  Upgrade your skills as you level up. There are three branches: Specialist, Soldier and Medic. Each one has features and bonuses appropriate for it's type. Choose which ones you want first to fit your play style or adapt it as you see fit (you get all of them eventually). Skills can be reset for the right price. Weapon upgrades can also be reset, you get nine points to allocate amongst two sequential branches and are a bit more limited. With weapons, resetting is free (at the time of this writing).  Mystery boxes (bonus items) which appear to be randomly dropped as loot, contain assorted items such as Extra Credits, Extra Experience, Upgrade Chips, One Ups (extra lives/continues) and the dreaded...Nothing! These boxes are opened after level completion, if you survive. Add in looted powerups such as Double Damage (a brief damage spree) and Nuke 'Em (damages all nearby enemies on pick-up) for extra fun and mayhem. Replay levels to improve your rating (up to three stars). Steam achievements (collect 'em all) and trading cards included.  __ Notes: This review is based on the reviewer's single player experience (finished level 30 in a bit over 10 hours). Multi-player has not yet been attempted. No game crashes were encountered although some issues with the game interface (weapon unlocks) have been noted while playing with a gamepad and require a mouse to respond.

In Warframe, you get to play a psychic space ninja, with guns, and swords, and lasers. It's also free to play, without locking content behind a paywall. That was enough to convince me to try it, and it was well worth the download! I've never once felt held back, or less effective, just because I didn't throw money at it. You can buy special currency with real money, or you can trade with other players for it; so even free players aren't prevented from getting things from the premium shop, like special skins or quality of life improvements (things like extra weapon storage, pet slots, crafting speed boosts, etc.)  The game has fast-paced, engaging combat, with melee weapons, throwing weapons, guns, lasers, flamethrowers, and more. There's a lot of content to explore. A LOT. And it's not all just running and gunning. There's crafting, minigames, pets, fishing, quests, and even a detailed storyline you can follow, if you want. All of these expand on the lore, and unlock new areas to explore, new features, even different modes of combat, like space flight, and a special one when you learn the secret behind warframes. I had always wondered how these armored space ninja suits worked. I won't spoil that though.  I've had a lot of fun with this game. They are constantly adding new content and features, fixing bugs, and streamlining gameplay. I still haven't explored it all! So there's plenty to do, and more added with each update  For a more detailed breakdown, read on!  -Controls: First I'll say, the controls are incredibly responsive. I can empty a clip into an enemy while charging them, then whip out my blade, execute a combo for extra damage, then launch into a jump and escape with some fancy acrobatics, without ever getting stuck in a long attack animation, or even having to switch weapons. It's fast paced, without tedious slowdowns. It all depends on how quick your reflexes are.  -Gameplay: How the game plays depends on your selection of weapons and warframe. Your warframe determines your shields and health, as well as special abilities. You can equip a melee weapon, a primary ranged weapon, and a side arm. You'll get to try out and choose from some basic options when you start out, and there's well over 300 different weapons to choose from beyond those. There's a large variety of missions available. From simpler ones, like 'eliminate X number of enemies' or 'defend this point', to stealth missions to collect data from different mainframes, having to sneak past their cameras and guards, or racing through parkour courses, dodging lasers and evading traps.  There are a number of minigames like time based puzzles for hacking, or carefully carving out a marked area with a mining laser for a better yield. There's even fishing? Yep. Space ninja fishing!... You'll have to see how it works for yourself. You can unlock hoverboarding in one of the massive open world areas, and even flight missions with the Archwing.  -Progression: There are a number of ways to progress in the game. There's quests and storylines to unlock new features, and different warframes. You'll have to finish missions to move to the next ones, and meet certain requirements to unlock new planets. You can replay almost any mission as many times as you want. Storyline quest rewards are only given once though. Using a weapon or warframe to defeat enemies or accomplish objectives yields experience. Each weapon and warframe can gain levels, which increases their mod capacity. Mods drop from enemies - they enhance different stats, depending on what they're for. You can get one to enhance shields or health for your warframe, or a rarer one that enhances both. For weapons you can get mods that speed up reload time, increase clip size, or add elemental damage for example. You can recycle extra mods you don't need for points to level up other mods, increasing their effectiveness.  Graphics and game engine: I'm always surprised at how detailed the graphics can be without bogging down FPS. There's so much to see, from gritty interiors of battleships, to arctic tundras, overgrown forests, and expansive spaces of the open world areas. The character and enemy models are detailed, and intricate - I haven't noticed anything that really stood out to me as looking poorly textured or blocky, and it all runs smoothly without needing a top tier gaming system to do so. I've very rarely seen any slowdowns with a system not much past the minimum requirements. The ragdoll physics are also wonderfully satisfying when you can slash your enemies in half, or send bodies flying with high velocity bolts that nail them to walls.  Pros: -Space ninjas -Staggeringly expansive content -Easy to learn, but takes practice and skill to master -Beautiful settings to explore -Huge arsenal to arm yourself with -Very responsive controls -Hundreds of hours of gameplay -In-depth story and lore (all of which is optional) -Exciting combat -Dark and gritty setting, but not without humor -Extensive range of challenge (From simple levels with weak enemies, to difficult, complex challenges that require some serious preparation)  Cons: -Can often be very grindy to unlock higher level stuff. (For example, crafting custom weapons takes a lot of resources and time.) -Some areas can be hard to find a group for - particularly Archwing missions, which don't seem to be very popular. -Can be overwhelming with all there is to see and learn. -Fast-paced missions means a lot of players rush ahead - lower level group missions tend to be a race to the finish. Groups are not required though.  Conclusion: I would very much recommend this game to anyone that likes action based combat, or third-person shooters. It's a blast to play, and you're unlikely to run out of content to explore and things to do any time soon.

Let's get it out of the way first. Alien Shooter TD does very little to change the formula when it comes down to the Tower Defense genre.  The biggest change is that the towers are replaced with soldiers from 7 classes, using from the basic shotguns and machineguns, to huge energy cannons and flame/ice throwers, which can be upgraded with up to 6 passive skills, equipped with up to 3 weapons each, and the weapons themselves can be upgraded as well. The weapon upgrades are just stat improvements, and the soldiers' include (among others and stats) explosive shots (which they use automatically), so there's nothing mind blowing.  Alien Shooter TD includes 4 difficulty levels, and the main differences are the amount of enemies, the composition of the waves and the health they have. Those, plus the usual Survival maps, bring it up to 35 regular levels, and the promise of more to come.  People have been complaining about the reload mechanic, because yes, soldiers require ammo to shoot in Alien Shooter TD, and that costs money. Especially at the beginning of a level, you will often have to decide between reloading your soldier's weapon, buying a better weapon or getting another soldier. With patch 1.3 the devs included an option to auto-reload, as well as other nifty ones, like ordering a soldier to hold fire.  It does have some problems, like soldiers trying to shoot even though they can't actually hit anything from that angle, except the wall right next to them, the enemies sometimes get lost on the map and you have to wait for them to get back on track, and the game itself managed to crash twice in the hours of gameplay I spent so far.  After all that, Alien Shooter TD does nothing to draw into the Tower Defense genre if you're not already a fan, but if you are a fan of TD and of the Alien Shooter series, then Alien Shooter TD gives you the chance to slay hordes upon hordes of familiar enemies, all while you listen to the same epic soundtrack from previous games, at a more than fair price. Too bad you can't buy the OST...

I'm not normally one to bother writing reviews, but I feel the need to warn people away from this game in it's current state.  Satellite Reign is not worth your time and it is definitely not worth your money. This game is buggy in a way that seems specifically designed to generate as much rage as possible from it's players. Here's a list of the major issues I've experienced in my relatively short playtime:  [list] [*]Save file corruption. [*]Enemies following me across the map, causing endless attacks. [*]Permanently broken achievements, years after release. [*]Horrible progression and balance. [*]The final straw: after spending an hour on a single frustrating mission, I save and take a break. When I come back to the game, that one mission has reset entirely. All other progress was kept except that mission, which requires you to pay $5,000. [/list]  I so desperately want to love this game. I love the setting, the research, the open world, and the ideas behind the gameplay. Unfortunately the execution is so poor and the bugs so prolific that I can't imagine anyone making it as far as me and still defending it. I can only hope that the game was enough of a success to warrant a sequel that can address these issues, because this game hasn't received any updates in quite a while and I've lost hope that it's ever going to be fixed.

Fidèle de la série depuis le premier opus en 2000 (wwowwww 14ans !!!!!!) je ne serais que recommander ce jeux qui aujourd'hui atteint un niveau de maturité remarquable. Tout d’abord ce qui frappe avec EUIV c'est la durée de vie quasi illimité, en effet ont peux jouer 20 fois le même scénario et cela se passera de 20 façons différentes selon vos choix diplomatiques administratifs ou votre réussite militaire. Chaque scénarios peux être joué avec n’importe quel pays n’importe où dans le monde ce qui rend le jeu encore plus inépuisable. Visuellement le jeu a énormément progressé depuis le premier volet ou il était carrément moche, puis un peu moins moche pour le second, presque beau pour le troisième (3d) et carrément beau pour le quatrième avec en prime une ambiance sonore à la hauteur. Le jeu a aussi énormément évolué avec une interface beaucoup plus claire que par le passé et au niveau des mécaniques de jeu, comme la diplomatie qui s'est grandement étoffée (protectorat, processus d'intégration des vassaux....), le commerce avec l’apparition des routes commerciales qu'il faudra défendre tout cela conditionné aux points d'administration, de diplomatie et militaire que vous glanerez au fil de la partie. J'émet d’ailler une petite réserve sur la gestion des points de diplomatie qui est vraiment frustrante dans les processus d'intégration des vassaux car cela coûte horriblement cher et pour la France par exemple qui a un très grand nombre de vassaux cela devient rédhibitoire, d'autant que le grand nombre de relations diplomatiques et inévitable avec une telle nation, et cela consomme aussi beaucoup de points de diplomatie. Et pour parler des choses qui fâchent il y a selon moi un véritable point noir, les DLC, (Paradox semble y avoir pris gout) ils sont nombreux certains n’apportent pas grand chose mais personnellement cela me fait un peu râler de ne pas les posséder, et le jeux avec l'intégralité des DLC peux faire vite monter la note !!! Un autre point négatif, la gestion des troupes, ont produit des régiments de 1.000 hommes infanterie, cavalerie ou artillerie qui vont constituer des armées, et cela que l'ont se trouve en Champagne sous l'empire ou dans la province de Québec en 1630. Je m'explique effectuer un levée de 1.000 hommes dans une province métropolitaine en 1805 n'a rien de choquant, mais la même levée dans une province de l'autre coté de l'Atlantique tout juste constituée censé être peuplée de quelques centaines de colons voir d'un petit millier au mieux me semble assez ridicule d'autant qu'il sera possible de faire 10 levées de 1.000 hommes et même plus. Pendant un conflit nous pourrons donc observer des batailles de 20.000 Anglais face a 18.000 Français, et quand on sait que l’intégralité de la population de nouvelle France et de Louisiane cumulée n'a jamais dépassée les 80.000 dont seulement quelques milliers de soldats réguliers cela choque un peu. La possibilité de constituer des milices pour les armées coloniales aurait aussi été intéressante avec une prise en compte plus poussée des contraintes géographiques (topographie, météorologie...) La colonisation qui mériterait aussi d'être améliorée va apporter (avec le DLC Conquest of Paradise) la création de nations coloniales  (nouvelle Espagne, Nouvelle Castille, les 13 colonies) qui vont devenir (surtout avec l’Espagne) très vite incontrôlables car il n'est pas possible de définir leur niveau d'autonomie. Enfin les Révoltes sont a mon goût trop fréquentes et parfois incontrôlables, pour reprendre l'exemple de la colonisation, je viens de coloniser une île des caraïbes et 6 mois plus tard je me retrouve avec 12.000 révoltés, mais d'où sortent ils !!!????????? Voila, en conclusion même s'il est loin d'être parfais EUIV est un jeu unique qui progresse et devient plus accessible, moins élitiste que les opus précédents avec un une interface plus claire un visuel enfin agréable une ambiance sonore réussie et des tonnes d'heures de jeu en perspective sans jamais (presque) se répéter, comme dirait l'autre J’ACHÈTE !!!!!!   Points positifs : [*] Durée de vie quasi illimité [*] Visuellement beau (clausewitz) [*] Ambiance sonore réussie [*] Interface de jeu un net progrès [*] Richesse des mécanismes du jeu (diplomatie, commerce, religion, colonisation...) [*] Carte du monde fidèle [*] Un nombre incroyable de nations jouables  Points négatifs : [*] Beaucoup (trop ?) de DLC et la note peu devenir salée [*] Gestion des troupes trop simpliste [*] Gestion des points d'administration, diplomatie et militaire parfois frustrante [*] Révoltes parfois trop fréquentes et trop aléatoires [*] Nations coloniales totalement hors de contrôle (DLC Conquest of Paradise)

It's a tricky one. It's not a bad game... as a franchise tie-in. As a stand alone, it's still not bad, but it's not great either. It feels like half a game, if anything. The story is too quick, the characters aren't given time to grow and the enemies' motivations aren't explained. I would imagine that if you are a fan of the Halo franchise, and have played the other games, that this one would make more sense to you, but as a relative layman, I didn't get as much out of it as I was expecting.  I bought this on sale for a fairly reasonable price and got 7 hours of play-time out of it. Not the best return on an investment in a single player game. It feels like it was meant for multiplayer, with the SP campaign tacked on. This is certainly no Starcraft II.  So many missed opportunities for story telling and customisation. You had a great big ship at your disposal, but you never get to play with it. Novelty levels are rushed through and you're just dropped from mission to mission without any real context or attempts at immersion.  The units are well designed, the worlds are beautiful. Visually, this game is very well made and holds up well over time. That part is good. Alas, because it is a console port, controls are clunky and occasionally sluggish, units don't stand intelligently, can't be selected as a PC RTS player would expect and special abilities can be a pain to activate.  6.5/10. Buy if it's on sale and you've already played the good strategy games.

I wanted to love this game, really I did. I went in with so much anticipation, but I am very dissapointed. Leaving aside the bugs which have now made it unplayable - a fatal error after defeating Abaddon's champions which means that I can no longer progress, and another in the Necron campaign that quits during battles, there is also the fact that it's even less of a gameplay experience than the last one was.  Gone is the ship customisation, which I had expected to be expanded, not removed. There is no developing your admiral.  Even in spite of that, I was quite enjoying the 4x elements of the game, but again, these were simplistic. The whole thing feels half-done.   The ship designs are impressive, but if they were going to create unique ships to fight against, why can't we use the Imperial versions in the campaign? They let us use Phalanx in the tutorial, but so far there's been no sign of it again, and that would have been really fun to use in the campaign. Further to this, I saw Guilliman's flagship in the trailer, and I was expecting that to be another playable ship, again, no. What's the point of designing these fantastic looking ships and not letting us play with them in single player?  The Tyranid ships are impressive, they essentially desined a whole new line of ships, and they're really cool, which aggrivates me because why couldn't they have done something similar for the Necrons? Four ship models, and that's it. I was expecting a fleet's worth and got that. On that topic, would it have killed them to design a BC ship for Mechanicus and Space Marines? That was an annoying gap in capability.  Things they can do to fix it immediately: Fix that fatal error! All the other flaws, I can live with, but that one just ends the game. Make the super ships available in the campaign, that just makes it more fun, and that should be what they're about. I can't assume that they aren't available later in the campaign, they just haven't been available yet. Increase the prestige benefits, some of them feel lackluster, and not worth all the effort put into getting them. Increasethe fleet limit enough that I can have three Battle Barges ini the same Space Marine Fleet and four Battleships in an Imperial. I know that they seem reluctant to do this, but surely that's not so much of an increase? Increase the benefits of capturing and holding certain planets. Change the nature of defence missions. Why would anyone need to hold an empty strategic point IN SPACE? That makes no sense. Get rid of those stupid totems in the Abaddon's lackeys missions. Just think about how the mechanics of that would work for a second. Space is huge and 3-dimensional. Spire would just go above, below or around them. That's really dumb. Which leads us neatly to reinforcements. I can understand having a deployment zone in the beginning, but why can't I choose which ships reinforce me, and why can't they enter where I need them, rather than at the edge? If the enemy can jump ships into the middle of the field, then so should I. Again, this would make it more fun and not waste colossal amounts of time bringing all my ships back to the start to rendezvous with my reinforcements. Let us choose which of our ships to bring to the battle from our fleets rather than having the game choose for us. Multiple selections in the campaign, rather than having to move one fleet at a time, it's maddening, especially in the Necron campaign.  Things they can do to fix it long-term: Bring ship customisation back, again, that's just more fun. Make systems and planets more customisable, maybe something to make defence missions more fun, and less of a slog to do. Getting attacked every five minutes by something just interrupts the gameplay and getting story missions done. I'd suggest system defence ships so that your fleets aren't constantly bogged down defending systems, like a garrison almost, and fixed defences, preferably that you can deploy yourself. Admiral customisation. Let us choose special abilities. I never even use Spire's warp jump. Let us level them up.  I do enjoy this game, really I do, aside from the fatal errors. But once I'd been thrown out of my Imperial Campaign and started to look around, I discovered that it could have been so much better, deeper, richer and much more fun. I hope that the developers can do something, because a lot of these problems are easily fixed and can improve the game ten-fold.

It is the best game out there right now and 93 from Metacritic does not do justice- it should be more.  It is also a better RPG than Skyrim in my opinion and a huge improvement to the previous Witcher.  Apart from the story, which is already just great, my selling point was gameplay. Many of the tedious quests and stupid and dull sid activities have been avoided in this compared to many RPG or other games, so it is just a natural flow of story and action for 200 hours.  That is a big success.  You can ramble the unknown ? marks everywhere on top of that and not get bored really.  It is a lot less repetitive IMO than other games.   Story and the characters are much enjoyable and immersive.  You do care about them and try to take good decisions.  But it is not as morally complicated as before, so using your best judgement is mostly sufficient.  The RPG elements of Character leveling, alchemy and crafting are from very good, good to meh.  Good thing is you do not have to use all of them unless you go to the top difficulty.  The weapons and armor are plenty as well, but I just suggest you go to master witcher school stuff.  Buying and selling are ample if you want to avoid overweight.  Combat is not much difficult but I did not go to the hardest setting. This probably is wise as well because you would get overloaded and drop the game with all the missions plus restarts.  The enemies are various and you need to use and know multiple signs and weapons and styles. While they are graphically strong, I just did not feel intimidated with vampires much.  And for side game called Gwent- this is easily the most fun mini game I have seen and yes, it could even be the main game for some.  Just adds to the value.  Graphics, atmosphere, environment, just great.  Some things I did not like: some missions are too long (matrushka thing) and some conversations are too long. Even the moves of investigating, some cut scenes- it looks like these guys have spent their whole life on the game and they want you to do the same.  As mentioned, they can cut down crafting totally and you would not miss much. And the Inventory menu can still be improved for quickness.  DLCs are a seperate topic and I will rate HoS and B&W seperately,  but just to be clear, you should absolutely buy the GOTY version and play these two.  I will probably do a New+ in a year or so and that is my first time to replay a game.  Overall, whatever the price is, go ahead and buy this, but get ready to invest a bit of time in this geography.

Follow The Cpt Froggy Club Curator Page for plenty more![/b][/url][/quote]  Atomicrops: ~~~~~~~~~   Well, your life is about to change. Most people who want to leave the big city are usually looking for a sea change. In your case, you want to leave because you inherited your uncle’s farm somewhere deep inland. You always liked your uncle, and as you wander around the farm with one of his workers, reminiscing about some fun times while checking all the fruits, vegetables and animals on the farm, you find something totally unexpected. An underground Nuclear Bunker!  As you climb down into the bunker while joking with your uncle’s faithful employee that nothing extravagant ever happens around here, the nuclear Armageddon begins. The good news is that you own a farm now, and you have every intention of growing the best crop, whatever difficulties come your way.  You are going to be well served with Atomicrops!  Atomicrops is an action roguelike/bullet hell/farming simulation game developed by Birth Bath Game and published by Raw Fury on the 17th of September 2020 on Steam. The game is also available on Nintendo Switch, Xbox One and PS4.  What a surprising and amazingly addictive game this is is!  Your goal is to survive for up to ten years and grow interesting mutant fruit and vegetables each season, but it won’t be easy at all as you’ll have to fight mutants rabbits, other crazy monsters and bosses at the end of each of these seasons.   Each season consists of three days, including a boss fight. As you start a new game, you’ll choose one of five characters at your disposal; you’ll have one character first and four others to unlock. No matter who you choose, you’ll start with the same weapon, which is some sort of rifle that shoots green bullets. The day begins at dusk, and on your first day you’ll have a small patch in which to grow your fruit and veggies (it’s a good time to prepare the soil and plant your first potato seeds). Then you’ll have about two minutes to explore the other lots attached to your farm. Two of the lots will be accessible, and the other two will need repairs to the wooden bridges before you can access them.  You’ll find the repair kits in town, along with weapons, relics and other goodies.  As soon as you enter one of the lots, you are immediately greeted with chaos as you find small and large patches of land with sleeping mutant rabbits and monsters around them. Each of the patches will have goodies for you to collect, but you’ll need to eliminate the main enemies attached to these patches in order to collect your rewards. You can’t miss them as they have a pink face icon above their heads. The small patch usually has either pink squirrels where you can collect new seeds that they’ve dropped, or a wooden crate which holds pickaxes. The bigger patches will have more enemies to kill, but once they’re killed, you will have two items to choose from. You can choose between two different types of animal each time (there are several animals on the farm, as you know). It might be a cow, a pig, or a hummingbird, for example. But you might be tempted by a new type of animal, the firing turret.  Some large patches will have scrolls with information that will help you to help you grow or fertilise your soil (your patch), and other large patches will give you a choice of two skills. I love this because it is basically randomised every new game, and each game feels and plays differently. There are two other things to search for on each lot: the bushes (which hold fruits that you can pick without any labour), and the next broken bridge to repair so you can get to the next lots. However, it is always a good idea to come back to your own patch at dawn to harvest your crops before the night comes along.  At night, you’ll have to keep planting and defending your crops from three waves of enemy. It’s hectic as hell and so much fun! Each time you kill an enemy, it will drop part of its anatomy on the ground which you can pick up and use as fertiliser for your crops, making them grow faster or bigger. You can also plant hearts to regenerate your health, and roses so that you can flirt with other characters in town, and exchange the roses for goodies such as firing turrets, which you can plant on your patch. Use the pickaxes you collected to grow the size of your patch so that you can produce more goodies. When the night is over, you’ll make a trip to town.   Each plant you harvest will give you Golden cashews which you can use to buy repair kits, weapons and weapons upgrades, tractors and bags of seeds.  Roses are also a form of currency, and it will cost you a fair few roses to flirt with a character so that you can receive your goodies from them, or even get married! (But do you know how much roses cost? A lot these days!)  After the three days of hard work, you’ll see the mayor.  Depending on the quality of your harvest, you’ll receive some goodies, including the almighty Cornucopia which you can use to upgrade your farm before starting a new game. Oh, I forgot to mention. . . you only have one life; there are no second chances here! Absolutely brilliant!  The pixel artwork is colourful and delightful. The soundtrack will remain in your head throughout the night, long after you finish playing the game (especially the night-time theme) . . . it’s just Marvellous!! The game runs beautifully; it has been some time since I said to myself, “Just one more game” and then totally lost the concept of time. For me, Atomicrop is a BIG, SPARKLING GEM!  Positives: ~~~~~~~   +	Colourful and delightful pixel artwork +	Fabulous soundtrack +	Fun, challenging and extremely addictive +	Good variety of enemies and the boss fights are epic +	Stacks of upgrades and skills to pick up +	Every game plays differently +	Full control support +	Achievements  Negatives: ~~~~~~~~   -	No trading cards as yet -	You may receive a tap on your shoulder from your partner in the early hours of the morning 😊  Atomicrops: If the Nuclear Armageddon starts tomorrow, I am becoming a farmer! Don’t miss this absolutely SPARKLING GEM!  10/10  Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own! Follow The Cpt Froggy Club Curator Page for plenty more![/b][/url][/quote]  EARTHLOCK: ~~~~~~~~~~   Imagine living in a world where humans are being suppressed by some sort of superior beings. Twice as tall as any basketballers and twice as big as Mr. Universe. Not only that, they use an entirely new and powerful energy, unknown to our race, which they have managed to store deep in the middle of the sphere! But humans will always be humans, and start an uprising against the oppressing race. As the conflict turns in favour of the homo sapiens, nobody thought about how to control this energy. And yes, the energy implodes and initiates multiple cataclysms, totally transforming the layout of the planet, creating strange vegetation and strange talking animals. Imagine no longer . . .  you’re about to enter EARTHLOCK!  EARTHLOCK is an RPG with turn based combat system developed and published by Snowcastles Games and is available on the Nintendo Switch, PS4, Xbox One and on the Steam platform.   As you start the game, you’ll take control of Ive Lavender, a cadet of the House of The Great Wave and the daughter of their leader, The General Lavender. This first act, if I may refer to it that way, is a nicely designed tutorial on how to play during the turn-based combat phases. Then, Ive will disobey her father’s orders and take part in a scouting mission, and you won’t be able to select this character until a quarter of the way through the game, when she will reappear.   The main character you’ll be playing from here on is Amon, who is a scavenger, and with the help of his uncle and half men-half shark, will attempt to retrieve an artefact from the Zabirum Temple in the burning desert of Umbra. As I am writing this review, and after playing a solid 8 hours, I am around the 40% mark of the game and I must say, it is extremely entertaining; I will leave you to discover the rest of the story from here.  As with most games of this genre, you’ll meet characters in different locations who will give you quests (main or side quests) for you to complete, with a view to receiving a substantial number of experience points, thereby levelling up your characters quicker. However, you can explore part of the Umbra world as you wish, and will encounter all sorts of enemies to tackle in battle. If you face one creature per fight and win, you’ll be given standard experience points. But if you face 4 foe per fight, the experience points will be multiplied by 4 if you win, for example. You might also collect coins or objects as a reward. These objects can be sold at stores or utilised to craft new goodies on the Plumpet Island, home of the Frogboy character (I can’t believe I have my own Island in a magical world)! By the way, you can travel back to this Island anytime you like, as long as you find one of these majestic frog statues somewhere within each of the locations; you will be able to save your progress by clicking on them as well. You can swap from one character to another at any given time. In fact, you’ll be promptied to do so, due to the fact that one character can harvest plants while another has the ability to dig out treasure, for example. It’s very cool!  Oh, I nearly forgot . . . there are chests around each of the levels; make sure you reach them, as there are plenty of goodies inside.  Each time your characters level-up, they will be given one talent point. Every single character has a talent tablet which is a 5 X 6 square. Each character profile will be locked on the third square of the first row. Within these tablets, you’ll have a square with a yellow hexagon, and an image printed in the middle. They are your next character abilities, and they are usually not connected to your character profile. What you need to do is to connect your character profile (image) to these squares with talent points you earn by levelling up to access these specific abilities. As you place your talent square on the tablet, you’ll be given the opportunity to associate and upgrade further skills for your characters, such as magic, armour, combat and other interesting ones which I will let you discover.   You’ll also receive extra talent points when the bond between two character grows within the combat phases. You’ll see stars appearing within the character interface.   Each of the locations will end with a boss fight, and let me tell you, it will not be easy at all. There is a trading post north of Zaber where you can redo some side quests and accumulate experience points quickly. You’ll need it. I just managed to destroy the boss of the burning desert, but then one kicked my butt rather quickly -I thought I was fighting super woman!  Graphically the game is very polished, and the soundtrack includes over 30 tracks. You’ll be able to play the game either with your keyboard or gamepad. I find myself travelling back to my island because I like it, but to craft items over and over again. Apart from that, the game is a little jewel!  Positives: ~~~~~~~   +	Great cartoonist graphics +	Stacks of enemies +	Entertaining story +	Fun and challenging combat phases, especially with the bosses +	Over 30 soundtracks +	Achievements and trading cards +	I have my own Island - go the Frogboy!  Negatives: ~~~~~~~~   -	I find myself going back and forth to my Island crafting items a bit too often.  What an excellent RPG; EARTHLOCK is well polished and thoroughly entertaining. I invite you to discover the world of Umbra!  8/10       Key provided by developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own! Follow The Cpt Froggy Club Curator Page for plenty more![/b][/url][/quote]  Giant Life: ~~~~~~~~   Every now and then you might experience a crappy day. From the time you wake up until the time you lay your head on your favourite pillow, it seems that these specific days just get worse by the minute. It might be a combination of several things that happen throughout the day, and they are amplified if you feel sick. For me, when one of these days arise, I always wish I was a giant, taking my revenge out on all the pitiful people who contributed to my bad day, squashing them and destroying everything they own. As a matter of fact, I had one of these days today! So, if you are in the same situation and need to let off some steam, I invite you to do so in the land of Giant Life!   Giant Life is a VR action/casual game developed and published by Patagoniart, and has been available on the Steam platform since the 8 of June 2019.   The game is composed of a tutorial and 22 levels. Your goal is to destroy all the buildings in each of the levels to win one, two or three golden stars, and to amalgamate as many points as you can. To do so, you’ll need to destroy buildings at just the right moment (when people nearby) in order to squash them with blocks of rubble and achieve the maximum number of points.  But how do you destroy these buildings, you might ask? Well, it’s rather simple; as a giant, all you need to do is to throw rocks into the buildings. You’ll have five different types of rock: a normal black rock (which will destroy a house as soon as it hits the target), a rock with a blue light field that explodes into four little stones that fly out in four directions when it hits the ground (these rocks are very effective if you manage to drop them right in the middle of several buildings), a rock with a yellow field that explodes into three smaller rocks in mid-air when you activate it with the trigger button on your control (they are quite effective in destroying houses or boats that are located at a certain distance), a rock with a green light field that will bounce once when it hits the ground, and a rock with a purple light field that becomes bigger as it travels through the air.  At the start of each of the level, you’ll be located on a hill with the village and its villagers right in front of you. On your left, you’ll have a bowl holding a certain number of rocks. The first few stages are easy, but as you progress to different levels, you’ll find that the villages also have buildings and fortifications. You’ll also have boats to destroy occasionally. Bear in mind, you must have at least one golden star to unlock the next level.  The game looks very good graphically and it is a lot of fun to play, but it is repetitive. I also found that on some occasions my aim was not quite right, (yes, yes, I can hear you all saying, “You can’t throw a rock properly, you old fart”, and you’re right). But then again, sometimes you totally miss a throw and the rock still hits a target! I skipped this one back in 2007. Lost Planet came along in a post-Halo-2 era when there was a whole raft of console-focused sci-fi shooters trying to steal Halo 3's thunder. Killzone, Resistance, Crysis, TimeShift, and on and on. It was easy to lose one in the onslaught, though Lost Planet does try for something a little different: a pyrotechnic, anime-inspired third-person adventure that feels like a sloppy mash-up of Metal Gear Solid and Gears of War.  The Good: * The level design-- where you're often frantically hopping into a stolen mech right in the middle of a pitched battle and then ejecting out again as it gets blown up around you-- is rad. Titanfall obviously cribbed some notes from this one. * The game still looks faaaaantastic with the graphic settings cranked up. The snow, dynamic shadows, smoky explosions, & even the fur trim on your coat still looks impressive. * The cut-scenes are anime af, while still telling a story that's way easier to follow than a Metal Gear plotline  The Bad: * Boss battles often seem more difficult than they're supposed to be, because of sloppy controls or bad camera placement. (Why the hell can't you go first person while piloting a mech? Too often you're blindly firing at an enemy while staring at the back of your own armor.) * The basic enemy soldiers are laughably bad shots, like stormtrooper-level bad. This is fun in its own way, but can make some stretches a little tedious. * That straightforward storyline sometimes runs a little *too* obvious, and left me wishing for a bit more Metal Gear weirdness.  Not much else to add. Surprisingly recommendable!

Спустя 5 лет не смогли толком улучшить игру, да и я бы на самом деле сказал, что где в чем то даже по графике ухудшили. Начнем хотя бы с того, что модели персонажей стали силиконовыми с блестящей кожей как у кукол, да и в роликах видно, что более менее постарались над прорисовкой только главного героя, но чёрт возьми его костюм просто ужасен по сравнению с костюмом из второй части. Из группы разработчиков отвечающих за графику можно похвалить лишь людей отвечающих за зрелищность взрывов, вот тут они постарались на славу и на мой взгляд достигли совершенства. Хочу также обратить ваше внимание на чрезмерное количество голубого и синего цветов, голубой самолёт в начале игры, голубой вертолёт в начале игры, джинсовый комплект одежды Рико тоже сине голубой, да даже часть ствола его оружия голубая, его друг - Марио, уж не знаю голубой ли, но как минимум его одежда точно голубая, голубые повстанцы и их транспорт (но их форму и транспорт могли сделать как цвет фракции, ведь во второй части именно так и различали фракции (красный, желтый, синий)), и все это на фоне голубого неба. Нет я ни в коем случае не против использования голубого цвета и его оттенков, но не в таком же громадном масштабе, чтоб аж затмить само солнце. Лучше закройте глаза, когда в начале игры вам дадут вертолет иначе вам придется узреть ужасно проработанную траву которая идеально развивается от ветра создаваемого лопастями вертолета, но тут вы сразу же заметите, как трава халтурно проработана, реально ухудшили графу, трава из нормальной превращается в траву из GTA 3. Рико больше не похож на скорпиона, скорее на Чака Норриса, только шляпы не хватает. Физика и управление автомобилями такое же де*рь*ми*ще как и во второй части, вот прямо без изменений, ну серьёзно, 5 лет прошло а управления авто хуже чем в Driv3r (если кто помнит эту игру, там хотя бы были проработаны такие мелочи, как возможность оторваться колесу на ходу у автомобиля, да и в принципе там ездить было не так то уж плохо. Да и в принципе управление почти не меняли, ну разве что в худшую сторону немного. А по поводу физики - чтоб вы понимали скажу так - на ретро автомобилях повернут на скорости почти не возможно, даже на средней, нужно около 5км в час сделать, чтоб это го*но развернуть, на мотоциклах вообще ездить не реально, ткнул на скорости кнопку поворота и мтцик развернулся аж на 45 градусов, ну тоесть если ты просто хочешь объехать какой нибудь встречный авто, то обязательно через леса и поля. Спортивные авто на удивление более менее сбалансированы, но у них тоже физика стремноватая. К самолетам, вертолетам претензий нет. Есть проблема с некоторыми лодками которые вроде плывут, а мы стоим на месте. Физика парашюта поменялась, он стал плавнее и медленнее, хотя во второй части мне нравился парашют больше. В этой игре полеты на парашюте и вингсьюте самая ходовая вещь, хотя иногда бесит, когда Рико не может лететь на крюке туда куда я его запустил, а может банально в забор скажем упереться, хотя тот справа от него стоит, опять же физика. Больше всего расстраивает, что в таких играх еще и гонки делают, кстати сдесь ребята тоже отличились, а именно количеством очков и таймером, на некоторых заданиях норм, а на некоторых впритык и после такого хочется спросить, а вы ребята сами то пробовали в своей игре на 5 звезд гонку на катере пройти который дан по дефолту, да еще без нитро? Просто как бы при гонке на катере я прошел трассу идеально и с нитро и при этом на 4 с лишним минуты больше требуемого. Посмотрел статы всех катеров и понял что такие гонки можно пройти только на Лучадоре. Отсюда вопрос, а зачем рекомендовать катер, на котором это можно сделать только при максимальной раскачке нитро? Неужели ради того чтобы люди эти гонки минимум по 2 раза прошли? (Так как без звезд не будет нитро.) В общем как я понял, разрабы проработали взрывы, поработали над саботажами и некоторой другой зрелищностью, а на остальное подзабили, и так вон 5 лет думали что можно туда добавить нового, правда кроме сюжета и нескольких новых фишек ничего нового не надумали. Складывается такое впечатление, что из всей комманды над игрой работали только пиротехники. Может им всю игру доверили клепать, поэтому такая лажа вышла? Блин, да тут даже сюжет на сюжет из второй части похож. все тоже самое, только модельки пластиковые и взрывы офигенные. Я честно не понимаю почему у игры столько положительных отзывов, ведь с первой минуты игры видно что ничего особенно нового в ней не появилось и уж если на то пошло, я лучше прошел бы ее с графоном из второй части. Да и по авто, могли бы уж у кого нибудь из конкурентов с*п*и*з*д*и*т*ь хотябы чутка физики, ну реально, машина почти не поворачивает, с такой физикой только по прямой катить. А еще такое ощущение, будто тачка поворачивать начинает не сразу, как ты нажимаешь кнопку а с задержкой. Во второй части эти косяки еще были простительны, потому как игра для тех времен норм получилась, её за одну лишь идею полюбили массы, а тут мы видим, что эта идея никак не совершенствуется. Еще по поводу багов и недоработок и оптимизации. Баги - тут их полно и никто не будет их фиксить. Да вспомнить даже корову на копоте машины у моба которая еще и ходила на месте. Я 1 раз провалился сквозь текстуры. 1 раз у меня не хотели прогружаться локации и объекты, а из за этого ничего нельзя разрушать, пришлось перезапускать. Игра периодически вылетает сама по себе без багов. Вот начал ты задание и игра вылетела без ошибок! По поводу оптимизации скажу, что жрет она оперативки гараздо больше заявленного в минимальных системных требованиях, там написано что на минималках 8Гб хватит, но я проверил через прогу, игра жрала от 10 до 14Гб, в основном во время боя и разрушений сооружений. Рукож*опы, одним словом! Кроме конечно тех кто взрывами занимался, вот кто реально там из пряморуких остался. Физика была ужасна во 2й части, но по тем годам это было простительно, в этой части увы физика только ухудшилась. Рико стал медленнее, крюк подтягивает словно в слоумо, спортивное авто не может повернуть на скорости, видно, что колеса повернуты, но тачка едет прямо, потому что вы не сбросили скорость, если машина в воздухе, то вы словно в невисомости можете крютить ее как вздумается, гонки стали еще ужаснее чем во 2й части, там они хотя бы не так бесили. Серьёзно, я игру выключил после того, как увидел что тварится с моим авто в воздухе, тоесть я с трамплина на нитро должен был лететь прямо, а вместо этого тачку начало крутить вертеть и она улетела кудато влево, хотя я идеально ровно прыжок сделал. В этой части я пока только один плюс выявил, это взрывы и разрушения, судя по всему это все что смогли за 5 лет улучшить разработчики.
