I have bought the game back in November/December 2014. I liked the period, but was a bit sceptical, especially when combined with a paypal payment method and was just willing to try it.  How much was I mistaken. It is my most played game on steam right now. I did hunt AI ships alone. I did chase player ships off the perceived turf with a group. For a time I was the one of lucky few, who were able to build HMS Surprise. I did successfully trade iron, when there was almost none left in the whole carribean. I went to the edge of the world. I met people that were nice and crude, honorable and dishonorable, dauntless captains as well as cowards. Does this appeal to you? If yes, this game might be just for you.   HOWEVER, you have to be willing to overlook some substantial flaws, at least for a time. Terrible UI. No help, if you don't search for it/ask. You have to be willing to accept behavioural standards of the community (courteous, gentlemenly). You have to be willing to learn. You have to be able to think of the battles as battles, not as the grind.   2nd HOWEVER, you get an opportunity to participate in the development of the game you have been waiting for for the last 10-15 years, due to the great devs, who really listen. (I can pinpoint some features that are in the game to originate with specific players and specific posts on the forums).  I will not tell you if the game is right for you. For me, best 40 EUR I spend on a game. For an early access title 9/10.

It probably serves me right for playing Oxygen Not Included for about 500 hours over the last couple of months, but this game just doesn't do it for me.   The gameplay is so shallow I was looking at my phone within half an hour, and so catastrophically bored within 2 hours that I left it running and went to get a coffee and watch TV. Nothing much had improved by the time I dragged myself back to it, so I binned it.   I love a good bit of zen gaming. I can harvest virtual fields for hours, drive virtual trucks for days, even disassemble virtual cars, switching my brain firmly off and just enjoying making something happen. I love a bit of god-simming and will happily build cities, or mars habitats, or roundhouses for days, worrying about where food is coming from or why my dupes are suffocating so much. I thought I'd love a bit of tycoon gaming....but this glorified dot-to-dot where the toughest challenge is getting tracks to go where you tell them to, is too infuriating for zen gaming and too paint-by-numbers-simple to engage the brain like a god sim.   Maybe I'm not a tycoon kinda guy, but wow that was dull.

Amusingly, for this sale, I decided to try out three dungeon crawlers and give them each 30 minutes or so to see if they were fun and if their user interfaces were clear.  This is the only one I didn't refund (Stranger in Sword City and Winged Sakura: Demon Civil War were).  Note on this review, I haven't finished the game yet.  Things may change.  The Good  - The user interface is cleanly designed and easy to immediately read and navigate. - The mini map is quick to look at and figure out what's going on in. - Combat is simple at first glance, with a few complexities that place it around Pokemon gen 2 in difficulty to understand.  - Even then, the in game menus and tool tips explain things quite nicely. - The game was immediately fun for me, once I got out of all the dialogues. - The game is quite similiar to Pokemon.  The Netural  - Art style is the same Sakura art style that everyone has come to expect from any game titled as such here on Steam.  The artist(s) could do with improving the looks of the women to not look so cookie cutter.  I will say that the backgrounds are nice and I do tend to look around them a bit more then is needed given prior dungeon crawler games. - While the game is not programmed in an RPG Maker, the combat animations look like they've been copied and pasted from it. - The game is an immediate grind fest.  Levels are not easy to aquire as XP is earned in one of three ways, each way gives a very low amount.  (( Levels are gained by being an attacker, by defending against attacks, and by just being there (which allows the party members not fighting to gain some XP should they ever be used again).) - This game is a very basic dungeon crawler in all respects.  The Bad  - Grind fest.  I know I put this as a netural, but due to an immediate lack of different enemies to fight, the first two to three levels of the dungeon are boring.  Once you get to level 4 and beyond, there's more enemy types and combat gets more exciting. - The dungeon is of a fixed designed.  Play through and explore everything once, you'll know where everything is.  There's no randomness outside of combat. - The game is similiar in design to how Pokemon Gen 1 is, if you started off with Charmander or Pikachu.  Level 2's boss monster is heavily resistant to physical attacks.  Followed soon after by level 3 being filled with them.  Kinda like Brock and then Mount Moon with its Rock types.  - No character generation.  You don't design your characters and they level up automatically.  The only customization you get is appearance for the two main characters, attack scrolls (TMs), and stat boosting seeds.  Overall and with my experiences thus far, I do recommend this game if you're a fan of old school Pokemon, dungeon crawlers, and don't mind the constant fanservice that all Sakura titles have to date.

This game makes me rage.. But I love it!  Firaxis studios' remaking of the older XCOM franchise is a great game all around without a shadow of a doubt. It has aliens, guns, global terror and addictive tactical play that I just can't leave alone.   The premise is simple enough, you're an operative for the XCOM organisation, and it's your job to direct the forces at your disposal to best serve the interests of humanity in fighting off the alien menace (more on them in a mkinute). You do this through turn based tactical combat scenarios and a metagame of base management and decision making that overarches the main gameplay by forcing you to choose which options you want to research, what facilities you want to construct to better your force or gear, and which missions you want to send your recruits on to shoot the aliens to bits.   At the basic level, that's what the game is all about really - decision making. It's why it works so wonderfully, and also why it will make you rage but keep coming back for more. The turn based nature of the gameplay means you can weigh the odds of different approaches as you go and take your time to figure out the various angles and opportunities you have at each point. Squad cohesion is important in mission gameplay, and a poor choice of action or missed opportunity could see you paying for it down the line with your squad members, when alien plasma fries them. It forces you to adapt and overcome your enemies, predict the outcome of your options and make the best choices, whether that involves a squad wide attack to wipe out the enemy or (occasionally) sacrificing one member to allow the others to move to a safer position or escape (though you'll find that this is a painful lesson when it's a high level unit with helpful abilities that you lose however).   There's plenty to keep track of and experiment with too. Your different units have classes that affect their weaponry loadout (heavy units being armed with an LMG and Rocket launcher at the first level for example) and abilities that go along with them (in the case of the aforementioned heavy, suppression fire and usage of the launcher etc), so making sure that the different specialisations are utilised well is wise to be keep in mind while on a mission. You are free to choose who you want to field however, so if you find you don't really enjoy using a particular class or would rather take another sniper than a support unit for example, it's your choice.   Outside of mission play the decision making is just as important if not more so. You'll create a base layout with facilities to upgrade or improve your arsenal and construct your gear between missions, and keeping appropriate facilities close gives benefits so juggling everything or putting one plan on hold to get a different module placed first can provide bigger bonuses down the line. The different research tiers as the game progresses ramp up in power quite nicely and are satisfying to play with when you finally get to top tier weaponry and armor (higher tier armors especially offering some interesting options in terms of gameplay, IMO). All important research unlocks all these goodies so taking advantage of your time at the base to figure out which projects you want to take next is the other main aspect between mission play to keep in mind - neglecting any one aspect ofyour squad's equipment can leave you underequipped for some missions but researching the alien tech and recovered corpses etc is also important so as to discover their weak points, making it a fine balancing act.   So yeah, as the title said, it'll make you rage. When Corporal Bloggs pops his head round a blind corner only to get it melted by alien plasma fire unexpectedly you might want to shout, or swear, whatever floats your boat. But it's so satisfying to play that you'll just want to keep coming back to try again. Maybe Corporal Bloggs' brother will have better luck on point instead..

Within my first hour of playing Dragons Dogma I was beaten up by the town drunk. By the end of the almost 70 hours I spent with it, I was sizing up a trio of bandits with a smirk on my real-life face, knowing even together they were no match for my steel and the extensive training I’d received under some of the toughest knights in this beautifully recreated medieval land. This wasn’t merely a change in stats and equipment. Without a single spell or magic sword, Kingdom Come gave me the abundantly satisfying feeling of transforming from doe-eyed scrub to stone-cold killer. Warhorse’s tale of tribulation and betrayal shines brightest in the little ways it sells the fantasy of living in the Late Middle Ages. Not only are there survival mechanics that track hunger and fatigue, but every aspect of your character’s appearance has an impact on how NPCs perceive you. The biggest example is how clothes will accumulate wear and trail dust as you traipse through the wilderness, leaving nobles less than impressed with your scruffiness.  NPCs' reactions to your appearance extend beyond BO simulation.  This required me to frequently take baths, visit the laundry, and have my outerwear mended by a tailor to make a good impression. Keeping relatively clean isn’t a chore because bathhouses are easy to find, and you can always dunk your head in the nearest trough of water in a pinch. This extends beyond BO simulation: if, for example, you’re trying to be sneaky, wearing clothes that don’t make noise when you move and are dark in color to blend in with the shadows decreases your chances of being detected. Likewise, walking into an inn covered in blood with a sword drawn is a good way to intimidate people into seeing things your way.  All of this takes place in a large chunk of wooded, medieval Bohemia that shows significant attention to detail and is filled with little historical touches that help it feel like a real place. Towns, farms, and logging camps are all laid out with a strong internal logic and built on a scale that makes sense for a real place, as opposed to the standard RPG city in a game like Skyrim that’s designed to feel large, but really isn’t. And there are no loading screens between areas anywhere unless you’re using fast travel, which I always appreciate quite a bit in open-world games.  The fantasy breaks down a bit too frequently under the weight of bugs, though. Some are of the goofy, largely unobtrusive sort you’d expect from an open-world game of this size, like a shopkeeper’s head loading in after the rest of their body. But others are less of a laughing matter because they got in the way of gameplay in significant ways. There seems to be a tendency for staircases to randomly decide, “You shall not pass!” and moving between areas of different elevation in general too often results in getting hung up on invisible walls or even stuck entirety.  Worse, a handful of quests in the second and third acts had either broken triggers or missing quest markers, sometimes requiring me to backtrack to a save I made an hour or more ago and choose a different path through a mission to avoid the roadblock. That’s not unusual for a big RPG, but it’s exacerbated by the fact that just about the only ways to save in Kingdom Come are drinking a rare, expensive type of alcohol or sleeping at an inn or brothel. Autosaves are unforgivingly infrequent. Crashes were rare, but when they did happen the autosave system sometimes set me back just as far.  The combat behind it all feels kinetic, precise, and polished.  To Kingdom Come’s credit, the actors, scenery, and textures do look fantastic on the highest detail level – but unless you have an extremely beefy system, you probably won’t be able to enjoy it that way. The PC version (which I’ve played on exclusively so far) isn’t particularly well optimized. To maintain a stable framerate in all situations, I had to turn down the graphics settings to the point where low level-of-detail models would remain in the scene for certain people and objects for a couple seconds even when I got up close, which was distracting. My PC (a Core i7-4770K with a GTX 1070) can run The Witcher 3 smoothly with everything cranked up, which made this especially surprising.  Luckily, the combat behind it all feels kinetic, precise, and polished. There is a significant learning curve, but I’ve found it to be a lot of fun the more I got the hang of it. Warhorse’s designers seem to have struck the right balance between realism and practicality. Sword fights have a nice tempo and reward technical skill, quick thinking, and most of all patience. Over time, I got the same feeling I experience when I’m starting to master a new shooter or real-time strategy game. My character became a force to be reckoned with because I mastered the systems, not necessarily because my strength stat kept increasing.  The realism extends to the sorts of trade-offs you have to make for certain gear, which added some interesting strategy elements. Plate armor (in addition to making you stick out like a bear in a seafood restaurant as mentioned above) is very expensive to maintain and counts against your encumbrance, so a scrawny character can't even safely wear a full set. Full-face helmets protect better against often deadly headshots, but restrict your field of view and make it more difficult to keep track of multiple enemies. My gear choices were often as much based on what made logical sense for the situation as what offered the best stats, which was another welcome departure from the standard RPG playbook.  Mounted combat feels like an afterthought – ironic, considering the studio’s name.  A few parts of the combat system don’t work all that well, though. I never got any good at the fiddly archery system, but thankfully, I was never forced to. Mounted combat also feels like an afterthought, in that it’s functional but clearly not something Warhorse spent much time refining (ironic, considering the studio’s name).  The story is gritty, engrossing, and complex, though it tends to fall back on some old-fashioned ideas of medieval historiography in a couple of places. Notably, the Cumans, a nomadic Turkic people from the Western steppe, are treated as token foreigners at times and faceless, Stormtrooper-esque bad guy mooks at others. Characters go well out of their way to refer to them constantly as “barbaric” or “savage” – which is certainly how most of the native Bohemians would have seen them. But without ever being given any indication that it’s not that simple (literally every Cuman I met was an enemy who couldn't be reasoned with), it comes across as trying to paint the shades of complexity that made up relations between steppe and settled societies in this era as purely black and white.  By and large, Kingdom Come does the medieval era right.  Verdict There’s a shining suit of mail underneath Kingdom Come: Deliverance’s authentically medieval grime. Strong characters and storytelling, one of my favorite first-person melee combat systems ever, and special attention given to building moment-to-moment immersion come together as a mighty alloy that ranks among the most unique, memorable RPGs I’ve played in years. While a lack of technical polish occasionally caused me a good deal of frustration having to replay areas due to a bug or poorly-communicated quest objective, it’s the kind of adventure I didn’t hate replaying

Crysis 2, like the original is a first person shooter. The game was released in early 2011. It also follows on from the plot of Crysis 1 as well. Although you don't really need to have played the original in order to follow the story. Crysis 2 was also the first game to use the CryEngine 3.  The game play has all of the regular FPS style features. You play the role of a Recon Marine, called Alcatraz. You are able to customize your weapons to match the situations you are in, as well as customizing your suite to the same too. Crysis 2 is set in New York City, which is often referred to by many as an urban jungle. This does however offer various different tactical options when it comes to planning attacks; allowing players to navigate between floors and buildings, and ruined buildings.    We also see a few changes in the Nanosuit used by our character too; this time you are able to use more than one suit power at a time, the strength and power modes have been combined into the same mode, and the stealth suit has been improved slightly.  Crysis 2 has AMAZING graphics; this could easily pass as a game being released recently. If you put all of your settings up to full, you are going to be in amazement at how good this game looks. You will need a beefy rig to keep a steady 60 fps, but my oh my it is worth it.  I sadly see no replay-ability in Crysis 2, there are the addition of a couple of difficulty modes, but to be honest; once you have played it the once, there is no reason to play it again. The single-player campaign is a decent length though - we are looking at a 18 hour long story mode which is very good for an FPS.  Thankfully I had no technical issues with Crysis 2 (unlike I did have with the original), I was able to play with every graphical setting on ultra and still had 60 frames the whole time. The only thing I will mention is there is no longer any multiplayer support since GameSpy shut it's servers down in May 2014.  If you enjoyed the first Crysis game, you will basically enjoy Crysis 2, it's the same just with even better graphics, more compelling story, and stellar FPS action and did I mention the amazing graphics? People may think £20 is a bit steep for a game of this age, however I am completely happy with this price as it almost fits into the £1/hour ratio.   1) Stay away 2) Only recommended when on sale [u]3) Recommended[/u] 4) Highly recommended 5) This is a must play  If you found this review helpful, please consider giving it a thumbs up. XCOM 2 is a turn based tactical strategy game, releasing on PC in February 2016. The game is a direct sequel to XCOM Enemy Unknown which was released in 2012. XCOM 2 was developed by 2K Games and Firaxis Games.   Like the first game, game play is separated into two. A management style simulator of controlling your base, and technologies inside it, whether it be through engineering or scientific research – allowing you to advance certain aspects of your base how you choose. Along with the base management side of the game, there is also a map style function which is where you move your ship around the world to different locations, or hubs of activity. Whilst on the map you will see side missions, your main missions, scrap piles to explore for extra money, along with a plethora of other activities to take part in.   The main mechanic in XCOM is of course the tactical squad based game play.  This squad of soldiers can consist of five different classes, which again can be specialized even further by using the skills tree which you earn points in through promoting your squad members. To begin with the classes start out very much the same apart from the weapons that they use. After you have gained a few promotions with the characters you will start to differentiate the classes quite a bit with the abilities they will gain. The actual in game mechanics are very much the same as the previous version of XCOM, but just with general improvements. The game’s cover base system works really well, with some handy UI enhancements that make it easier to see how the cover affects you.  What I wasn’t too keen on was the aiming mechanic. On countless occasions I found myself face-to-face with a foe, and still my percentage chance to hit them with my gun would be around 30%. I know there is always going to be a chance anyone will miss a target, but c’mon, these are trained soldiers in point blank range, it shouldn’t be that low. This became increasingly annoying as you progress through the game onto harder enemies which make a habit of getting up close and personal with you.  Overall I found the game play in XCOM to be really intuitive and very addictive with that “oh one more turn” feel to it.   Graphically, XCOM 2 is a really stellar looking title. Absolutely crisp animations of anything that moves, right the way down to the rag doll effect of bodies when they get shot (or blown apart). It just looks so fluid that it feels real. The textures and character models are also really high quality too. Normally in tactical games like this the graphical element is more skinned down on to allow for more focus on the game play but not XCOM 2. It is one of the best looking games to come out in the past 12 months and one that will really challenge your rig if you want to push out max settings.  The voice acting is top notch too; I was a little disappointed that all of the enemies have the same kind of voice, but given that there is plenty of different enemies in the game to begin with, this can be forgiven a bit. I would have liked to have seen a little extra depth used with sound in the game mechanics; there is an element of stealth to the game play, at least at the start of missions. It would have been nice to have some sort of sound meter that would trigger alarms for the enemies if you made too much sound – again just a small improvement which would of made the immersion all that more deeper.  The game has varying levels of difficulty for the overall campaign – this of course is down to how hard you want the game to be.  After you have finished one play through of the game you will unlock “Ironman” mode which essentially saves your game after every action you take, meaning you cannot jump back a few saves if you messed something up. You have one chance to succeed and that is it. Given that the side missions in the campaign can make a real impact on how the rest of the game pans out, I see this as a really interesting game mode that has the potential to have endless amounts of replay ability. I have been playing for roughly 15 hours so far and I have just about finished my first play through. I will for sure be trying out the Ironman mode personally to see how hard it really can be. Where you start on the world map, and the in game maps are all randomly generated, so whilst the actual objectives of missions may stay the same, where you carry out those objectives will differ from play through to play through.   Technically, I had a couple of issues. The main one being I did get random crashes. A few of these caused my graphics drivers to crash. This stopped when I configured an SLI profile for my two 970s and helped with the overall performance of the game too thankfully.  I was happy enough playing on 1080p given the high quality of the graphics on show to begin with. My rig was not capable of playing at 4k, and to be honest I think you would struggle to find a rig to play any of today’s recent releases on 4k.  Whack you’re AA up to max and you won’t really notice a difference though.   XCOM 2 is by far the best game in the series so far; the graphical enhancement of the game, as well as the improvements made on the already core game play mechanics makes this a tactical turn based player’s wet dream. Apart from the technical issues I had, I have struggled to find anything major wrong with this release.  The game’s regular price tag of £34, 99 is the mark of this being a AAA release; the sceptics amongst us will want to wait for this to drop into the sales market but if you are keen to pick up where Enemy Unknown left off, XCOM 2 will definitely keep you entertained for plenty more hours with a greater gaming experience. So I just finished this amazing game and wanted to give my 2 cents both for the players that are thinking about getting it and for the developers in search of feedback. So here it is:  Gameplay: this is likely the best aspect of the game. No other CRPG has the many and unique features of DOS2, likely thanks to this game using its own engine. Unlike in other isometric RPGs, the game is fully in 3D and so it is possible to interact, move, grab and attack a large number of elements of the environment, allowing a lot of creativity when solving the problems that are presented to us. One of the most famous aspects of the game is the interaction between elements. Thus, the pool of blood left by an enemy being stabbed can be frozen with an ice spell creating slippery surfaces. Water can be electrified which will paralyze enemies and oil or poisonous clouds can explode if set on fire. The enemies are ruthless and intelligent, blessing the fire that you have placed around them and transforming it into a healing blue fire, or cursing the harmless pool of water at your feet to transform it into a lake of worms and disease. The duration of the game easily reaches 100 hours and the progression, although limited to resolving the 4 acts of the game 1 after another, is extremely non-linear within each act, allowing you to solve the situation at your own pace and your own way, which gives a lot of replay value. Also interesting how the game lets you kill every NPC out there and still find a smart way of reworking the main quest and at the same time create consequences for what you have done. DOS2 is all about freedom of choices, both gameplay-wise and narrative-wise, and their consequences. Added to this, a multiplayer mode that really lets up to four players to share a world and leave their mark on it.  Setting: the graphics are already over the top for isometric RPGs, but they could improve in how detailed are the models of, at least, the main characters. The world is instanced in 4 big maps, which are very open, beautiful and overall really well crafted, filled with detail and secrets that make exploration a rewarding and a very entertaining process. There is also just the correct balance between battles and puzzles, so both elements keep being interesting until the end without becoming a tedious experience. The cities feel alive and the NPCs wandering both the cities and the roads always have interesting (or at least funny) things to tell us and/or sell us, sometimes even presenting us an exciting side quest. The NPCs will react to us committing a crime such as stealing from their pockets or from the nearby table, confronting us in different ways or actively looking for the culprit if we are sneaking. Regarding the sound aspect, every dialogue in the game is dubbed (even the ever present narrator voice) which is remarkable, and the music gets the job done and even gets to shine here and there. As good as the setting is, things could still be added to make it even better, such as a day-night cycle and a weather system.  Narrative: the narrative aspect is likely the weakest part of the game, as it happened in the first game too. About its good points, I could say the story is delivered in perfect dosage, giving you pieces of the plot little by little, always avoiding being overly verbose, and shifting depending on your methods of approaching a problem, which includes which character you use for that. Also the game is filled with really entertaining side quests, and the personal quests of your party members are no exception, keeping interesting and relevant until the end by adding new objectives with each arc. Another interesting option is how the character creator lets you play as one of the party members giving us interesting replay options. Despite all this, the plot is however, not at the level of complexity of popular CRPGs, nor are the party members that, even with their very good side quests, just lack enough dialogue to avoid flatness. Same goes for the antagonists, that lack the relevance you would expect from them and never get to the point they should be, being physically absent for most of the game and sometimes even bordering the comical and the cliché in their scarce appearances.  In summary, DOS2 is one of the surprises of the year, and both its gameplay and its world should be the role models for the CRPGs to come. Regarding the narrative, there is still a lot of room for improvement.  If I had to quantify its quality, I would give it a solid 9.

The story is fun, and the culture and characters are interesting and fairly well rounded. The art style is beautiful and the presentation is top notch. This is a visual novel with one romance path at present. The game itself is simple and has very nice english voice acting.      The relationships do feel rather organic and seem to flow naturally, I was pleasantly surprised. However, I find the odd ocassion, which also seems to be the case with other games, even Mass Effect, Dragon Age, and Deus Ex to some degree, where the choices you make do not always come across as you are expecting them to. To some extent this can be frustrating as there's very little explaination as to how your character might respond, and I admit sometimes I felt some of the choices I could make came right out of left field. For example, you might be presented with three dialogue choices to choose from, and the description of what your character might do or how they might respond can be quite silly or out right vague in one or two cases. However, in most cases it gives you a pretty good idea,but not always.  The game has a very enjoyable atmosphere  and I have thankfully not encountered any technical issues.The animations have had no slow down and I've yet to encounter any bugs.  I would highly recommend this game to anyone who's wanting a well presented, intereresting, and rather light hearted comedic take on the fantasy rpg visual novel. Personally, I was slightly disappointed by the finished game, after being so hyped for it in the months before release. I feel Creative Assembly should have kept more of the features from Rome: Total War that made me play it for over 450 hours. I feel     there were some major flaws (namely the fact most cities only had the capacity for 3 or 4 buildings) and I couldn't help but feel that Creative Assembly tried too hard to make the game different for the first in the series. But, without comparing it to its predecessor, Total War: Rome II is a good game for anyone new to the Total War franchise though I would advise against purchase if you are looking for a game as good as some of the previous total war games (namely Rome and Shogun II). Some features worked very well, such as the gravitas system, combined land and sea battles and multiple capture points for cities. Unfortunately, I am constantly reminded of this game's predecessor so my enjoyment of the game is clouded, but I feel it is a good place to start in the Total War franchise as well as the RTS genre in general

Моё знакомство с Hitman началось со второй части. До первой, так уж получилось, в то время руки не дошли. Сейчас после прохождения codename 47 у меня двоякие чувства. С одной стороны я рвал и метал, с другой - я восхищался ей. Сюжет как таковой прослеживается только в первой и последних миссиях. И, учитывая последнюю миссию, contracts подходит больше на продолжение, чем sillent assassin, несмотря на миссии-ремейки из первой. О агенте 47 в ней очень мало информации, и какое-то представление о нём складывается только в последней миссии. В современных играх игрока как будто водят за ручку. Здесь всё иначе: дают задание и мучайся как хочешь. Геймплейно она ничем не отличается от своих будущих игр. Есть несколько факторов, которые мешают прохождению. Первое это  управление: чтобы к нему привыкнуть, быстро ориентироваться в меню действий и метко стрелять по вражинам(кои очень метко и больно бьют при обнаружении) понадобилось время. Второе это непонятная система обнаружения - непонятно враги просекли тебя или нет. Иногда они видят сквозь решётки, иногда нет, сиди гадай. В одной миссии из-за шального выстрела парни на вышке стали невидимыми(это единственный баг, который встретился мне). Я очень долго горел, но потом это мне сыграло на руку. Ну и третье - дурацкая система возрождения. Сохранений в игре нет. Точнее есть точки, на которые ты переносишься, когда мрёшь. Смысла дальше играть в тихого убийцу после такого нет, только идти на таран. Бронежилет помогает только против пистолетов, автоматы его игнорируют. Но при всём при этом, не смотря на угловатую и уже непривычную глазу графику, играть в неё интересно. Задания также в разных частях планеты, уровни интересные и порой непредсказуемые. За музыку отдельное спасибо Jesper Kyd. Поиграл бы я в неё ещё раз? Нет, я бы ограничился одним разом. Благо большинство интересных уровней получили ремейк.

I find that I really, really like this Indie gem of a game. It is a story rich space RPG from a two man team of highly dedicated game designers. They keep adding to the game too, and it's all good.  The game itself has stylized space battles and squad skrimish. And what feels like a really complex and choice-rich story line. Making certain choices when interacting with some characters will not only affect that situation, but will roll on, shutting you off from other choices down the line and making still other trees of options available to you. There seem to be a wide number of routes through the actual story.  This single player game has RPG, levelling, upgradable spaceships, and retro style squad skirmishes. You hunt for people, carry prisoners, negotiate, trade, battle space pirates and make war with opposing factions. You curry favour with the different houses, and attempt to navigate the infighting and backstabbing.  Another thing; The customer sevice is out of this world. I mailed Andrew when I had a problem; the game would not load (though it turned out my own 2012 C++ had crapped out; because of reasons. It wasn't a problem with the game). Not only did Andrew answer but he actually helped me troubleshoot the problem until it worked. That is incredible! Thanks Andrew.  10 for effort 10 for re-playability 10 for service  This game will not be for everyone. The AAA-game crowd wont be happy with the lack of rapid moving eye-candies. But I like it precisely for its different approach and off-beat quirky nature.  I recommend it.

Seriennummer kann man per Internet aktivieren, den Registrierungsvorgang braucht man für den Singleplayer Modus nicht.   Zum Spiel:   Kapitel 1 ist große Klasse, man fängt klassisch wie in Gothic als Hanswurst an und levelt sich hoch. Am Ende des ersten Kapitels klatscht man aber die meisten Mobs schnell weg. Nur Gegnermassen (so ab 10 Mobs) bereiten noch Probleme. Es wird sogar erotisch, wobei ich die Dame nie wieder gesehen habe..oder habe ich die nur übersehen? Das zweite Kapitel ist asiatisch angehaucht, aber durch die englischen Namen usw. kommt das alles nen bisschen schräg rüber (Sprache ist ansonsten deutsch, keine Sorge), aber das war im ersten Kapitel auch so. Spielt sich nicht mehr ganz so flüssig wie das erste Kapitel. Das dritte Kapitel besteht im Grunde nur noch aus Untotenkloppen und einer überraschenden Story. Das vierte Kapitel ist dann noch mehr Monsterklatschen mit üblen Blockern und am Ende darf man dann sich in einem 10 Minuten Bossfight versuchen ohne das ansonsten freie Speichern nutzen zu können. Ich hab dankend darauf verzichtet und mir den Kampf und Schlußsequenz bei You...angeschaut.   Fazit:  Kapitel 1 = Top Kapitel 2 = Naja geht so Kapitel 3 = .... Kapitel 4 = Leute, wenn ihr schon keine Lust mehr habt, dann lasst wenigstens am Ende die Savegamefunktion drin.   Alles in allem hats schon Spaß gemacht. Hab einen Nahkämpfer gespielt, der die Keule von irgendeinem Endboss genommen hat und alles schön verprügelt hat. Die Keule ist so gut, die nutze ich sogar noch im Addon und hab immer noch nichts besseres gefunden. Grafik ist hübsch, der Held hat nen lockeres Maul und die Dialoge sind schön vertont und die Filme auch ganz nett gemacht. Wer Gothic mag wird 2 Worlds auch mögen. Bisschen Skyrimfeeling ist auch drin, aber eher Gothic. Kampfsteuerung ist nett gemacht, wobei die Todesstoßanimationen ruhig besser sein könnten, so kommt immer mal ne Deadszene und das Vieh ist noch nicht tot. Das ist bei Fallout 3 dann doch etwas besser ;-)

[h1]In the year 2525...[/h1]  G String was the Half Life 2 mod that I wouldn't shut up about during the golden age of HL2 modding. It offered a unique view to a dark future dystopian city environment that even today has no equal. Bladerunner might be a close example, but it's even darker than that.  Bought it instantly to support the creator for all the memories, but I'm in awe of how much the retail version has improved all across the board compared to the original mod. While still powered by the Source engine, it's a whole new experience even for a returning player. Graphics may seem dated to some, personally I don't mind them.  Navigating some of the levels is not straightforward as it's not always clear where you have to go, or what you have to do in order to progress. I think it makes sense as the way forward shouldn't always be obvious. I consider it part of the challenge and never had to spend too much time wandering around to the point of losing interest.  It's a creation made with love and I love it too! 8/8

Bioshock Infinite is one of the dullest shooters I played in 2013. I would be sad that I pre-ordered the game if it didn't come with a bunch of much better games.   The combat is boring. In previous games you held every weapon and could equip every plasmid at the push of a key. Now you can hold 2 underpowered guns at a time, and must go through an annoying wheel to equip a different vigor (plasmid). You can hold a very little amount of ammo, and since money is pretty hard to come across in the game, you will only be able to fully upgrade a few guns. Meaning you will find yourself in plenty of situations where you have no ammo or eve, and are screwed since all other weapons are underpowered, and enemies are complete bullet sponges.   There are skylines throughout the maps in the game. In the trailers these looked great, there were plenty everywhere, and they seemed to spice up combat a bit. In the actual game, there is a little one in some of the maps. They are pretty boring to use, and are almost nothing like what was shown in game demos.   You have a companion throughout the game who isn't so bad. She can open up 'rifts' which can benefit you in various ways. She also chucks you first aid, weapons, and eve vials every so often. But overall she does little to help improve the dull gameplay.   The story is pretty decent. You are taken to a city in the sky to find a girl to wipe away your debt. Then things start to get a bit crazy with the tacked on time travel stuff to make the game seem clever. I never finished the first 2 games, but from what I played of them, the stories were a lot better. There's not much else to say without spoiling the plot, so I will leave it at that. The story is okay, but it's nothing special.   Overall the game is decent. If you can get it on sale, it's worth it. But I wouldn't pay full price for it.

This game sort of exists for shock factor. Sadly it's not the best kind of shock factor either, the likes which you could find in great adult cartoons, or even so-so adult cartoons where they manage to tie it in for a narrative purpose, or at least it has a good punchline, but instead feels like adult content for the sake of adult content with a few shining moments in between.  The game play is mediocre and is mostly saved by the fact that it's relatively easy as long as you know to stock up on items before getting into the hard sections. I played on the default difficulty so I don't know how much harder things are on the higher levels (there's like 15 difficulty levels for some reason). Watching a let's play might be sufficient for seeing most of the hijinks that happens, but if you do desire to play it for yourself there are a handful of relatively unique interesting weapons that make it not completely bland combat. You can do some of the 'chores' without making a scene, and one of the main reasons I checked out the game, but I was under the impression you could do this with everything and unfortunately there's plenty of moments where you really don't have a choice but to get into FPS fighting. The worst part is that if you do start to try to do it without fighting until you have to you can easily end up understocked for when you do have to go in guns blazing (which happened to me but thankfully I skipped a lot of fighting by getting arrested). So if you do decide to play this for yourself remember: even if you try to avoid combat as much as you can, make sure to stock up on ammo and health items.

Nach etwa 300 Stunden, die ich mit Mount and Blade verbracht habe, schreibe ich jetzt endlich mal eine Rezi. Vorweg: Das Spiel und all seine DLCs sind jeden Cent doppelt und dreifach wert. Ich habe viele, viele Stunden mit dem Single Player von Warband zugebracht, einige mit dem Multiplayer, viele Stunden mit Napoleonic Wars und einige Stunden mit Viking Conquest. Alles sehr sehr lohnenswert und ein großer Spaß, sowohl Single-Player als auch Multiplayer.   Ein kurzer Blick zum Single Player von Warband. Man startet als kleiner Lord in einem der Reiche und steigt dann nach und nach durch die Erfüllung diverser Aufgaben und durch militärische Erfolge in der Hirachie des Reiches. Erste Lehen werden verliehen und irgendwann bekommt man durch eine erfolgreiche Eroberung die erste Burg bzw eine Stadt zugesprochen. Nach weiteren Lehen ist man zu einem mächtigen Lord im Reich geworden und bekommt keine weiteren Lehen mehr verliehen.... Offensichtlich ist man zu mächtig. Ja und dann... kann man versuchen ein eigenes Reich zu gründen, setzt sich gegen zahlreiche Feinde durch, erobert Burgen und Städte, vernichtet andere Reiche und wird irgendwann König.  Das zu Grunde liegende Kampfsystem ist sensationell und der hier präsentierte Kampf zu Pferde ist der beste seiner Art in einem PC-Spiel. Zumindest ist mir noch nichts besseres unter gekommen. Ganz egal ob in Assassins Creed oder bei bsp. Skyrim. Nirgends ist es so gelungen wie bei Warband.  Der bereits erwähnte Multiplayer ist ebenfalls sehr spielenswert. Insbesondere die verschiedenen Spielmodi machen immer wieder Laune. Hier sei insbesondere der Commander-Modus beim Napoleon-DLC erwähnt. Es macht einfach Spaß die eigene Einheit in die Schlacht zu führen.#  Ein sehr gelungenes Spiel für wenig Geld.  10/10

Here is my final review for the release game.  I had to change my thumbs up to down, but I hope someday to turn that back around.  First off, I love the concept of the game.  This game shows a lot of potential and I believe someday it will come through.  Second: the final release is missing key components that I would advise people to wait for at least a year, possibly two before buying the product as it.  The first issue is Game Master management.  Game master management is an essential tool for running an MMO, MUD, or other server in a way that an end user playing the game cannot understand.  To keep GM workload under control you should have a a screen that runs seperate from the game, you need to have extensive user control tools that allow the game master to isolate and talk with a problem player, to record chat and actions on selected players, and increase or decrease stats, plus run server variables and camera shadow players.    The second issue is that the building art is limited.  In a game where you do not hand design buildings, you should be able to reset building facades. This is not implemented.  Third, while there is a coin system after a fashion, there should be a GM controlled money system in place.  Again this should be handled by a control panel.  Finally, under the hood there is an extensive guild relations tools available, but there is no way to use them.  This game WILL be a winner, but wait for the GM tools to mature before jumping in.

Fabuła i klimat. Dwa słowa oddające charakter tej gry. Choć rozwój fabuły w dużym stopniu toczy się przez oklepane już znajdowanie różnych wiadomości, tudzież starożytnych napisów, można uznać, że w tym wypadku jest to ok - jest to dość typowy już ostatnio kompromis w grach eksploracyjnych czy walking simulatorach, który mnie na szczęście jeszcze nie zmęczył.  Co więc w tej fabule mamy? Lądowanie na obcej planecie, która okazuje się skrywać swoje tajemnice - szybko okazuje się, że istniało na niej inteligentne życie, co oczywiście wzbudza ciekawość - czy nadal gdzieś ono istnieje, a jeśli nie, to co spotkało tę dawną cywilizację?  Nie można powiedzieć, abyśmy otrzymali jasną odpowiedź na wszystkie nasuwające się pytania, dlatego na stronie gry toczą się długie dyskusje dotyczące interpretacji pewnych zajść. Nie jest jednak tak, że gra zostawia nas bez żadnych odpowiedzi, co prowadziłoby do frustracji - jest to w tym wypadku raczej pozytywne, gdyż wciąż myślimy o grze po jej zakończeniu.  Klimat z kolei jest niesamowity. Sporo czasu spędzimy w podziemiach, rozświetlając sobie ciemności pochodnią lub latarką, a to na co w nich natrafimy będzie budowało atmosferę grozy. Chwilami gra przypominała mi wręcz dungeon crawlera - tylko bez walk. Nie jest to jednak horror straszący w sposób nagły - nic tu nam nagle nie wyskakuje na twarz - a poprzez długotrwałe budowanie atmosfery samotności i nieznanego. Nie dostajemy do rąk żadnej mapy, a opcjonalne ukryte jaskinie potrafią być skomplikowane w budowie i ze dwa razy zdarzyło mi się na trochę zgubić, co w zasadzie też sprzyjało klimatowi - czy uda mi się znaleźć wyjście nim skończy mi się woda?  Gameplay dostarcza wiele przyjemności, choć należy tutaj nadmienić, że nie jest to prawdziwy surwiwal - to tylko gra eksploracyjna z jego elementami. Wody i jedzenia znajdujemy tak duże ilości, że w zasadzie stają się elementem pomijalnym, przyjdzie nam jednak mierzyć się z bardzo uprzykrzającymi życie (ale nie rozgrywkę) warunkami atmosferycznymi - nie zawsze będziemy mogli pozwolić sobie wskoczyć do wody, żeby nie przemarznąć, a niejeden raz dostaniemy w głowę odłamkiem meteorytu, jeśli w porę nie schowamy się za zasłoną. Przejście gry nie stanowi jednak trudności, nie jest też zręcznościowo.  Pod względem wizualnym gra stoi na wysokim poziomie - nie ma się naprawdę czego wstydzić (wykorzystano silnik Unreal 4), na laptopowym GTX 1060 śmiga płynnie na najwyższych detalach, zatem optymalizacja jest ok. Pod względem audio jest jeszcze lepiej.  Do czego mógłbym mieć zastrzeżenia? Ja chętnie zobaczyłbym tu jakieś skomplikowane zagadki (jestem fanem dungeon crawlerów, a już szczególnie Legend of Grimrock II), ale tych zasadniczo nie praktycznie żadnych, a już na pewno nie trudnych. Niektórym może nie spodobać się to, że mamy tu tylko iluzję otwartego świata - tak naprawdę gra jest liniowa i nie mamy też wpływu na jej zakończenie. Dla mnie nie jest to wadą, raczej lubię gry, które stoją na pograniczu gry i filmu, po prostu w ładny wizualnie sposób, opowiadają ciekawą i klimatyczną historię, nie zmuszając mnie do zręcznościowych wygibasów (np. SOMA). Jeżeli szukacie surwiwalu - nie tędy droga. To tylko wciąż (rozbudowany gameplayowo) walking simulator.  PS Jeżeli posiadasz - instaluj grę na dysku SSD. Ja wrzuciłem na HDD i ładowała się dość powoli. Po przeniesieniu na SSD czasy ładowania są do pominięcia.  PPS Gra zajęła mi ponad 20 godzin, ale ciężko powiedzieć ile dokładnie - steam nie liczył mi czasu gry w trybie offline. Niestety - to raczej bug, ale w trybie offline większość osiągnięć steam nie zostanie zaliczonych!

This is the epitome of a pay-to-win game. So much so in fact that the entire game is, in essence a pay-to-play game, and blatantly so, with its pop-up cash shop that constantly overwhelms you (after logging in, or in-between games, or simply if you leave the game playing). Considering how often you are 'offered' the chance to spend real money in order to progress (unless you spend hours a day playing and never miss a log-in reward) I was surprised at how expensive the items for sale are. It's not only annoying, it's also ridiculously overpriced.   Even discounting the real money angle, the gameplay itself is technically awful, even though it's good graphically. It's pretty to look at, but awful to play. The scoring mechanics are completely unbalanced and don't make much sense. Left over turns are worthless most of the time, but on some levels are everything you need to pass. It's hit and miss as to what things are worth in the game, and the 'special' items don't always parse their value correctly. By this I mean the items created by matching four-of-a-kind and so on.   I have played some pretty awful match 3 games before, and this one ranks among them. It's honestly unpleasant and tedious to play. It feels like a Facebook game with everything that you would have had 'friends' send you up for grabs in the cash shop.  I have spent a long time playing this game, trying to find something redeemable about it, but at this point it feels like a chore to play. I'm sorry, I gave it my best shot, but I honestly cannot force myself to continue and complete this game.

Иногда хорошую задумку губит отсутствие должного финансирования или/и недостаточная компетентность разработчиков. Как это случилось и в разрезе данной игры. Идея неплохая, нарисовано само по себе неплохо, даже годные секреты есть, но подано из рук вон низкокачественно, и подано абсолютно непроработанно. Ощущение от книжки — словно жрёшь овощной суп на воде. Вроде как пожевать чота есть, но в целом сплошная пресная вода.       В ВН что главное, помимо сюжета? Уровень интерактивности и логической взаимосвязи ветвления происходящего. В «Купидоне» за видимостью прорвы вариантов опций выбора кроется совершенно неочевидная степень изменения сюжета. Герои говорят и ведут себя одинаково, абсолютно линейное развитие происходящего. Только в финале становится видно, изменилось ли хоть что-нибудь. Если что-то и меняется, то на одну-две реплики, ничего сверх. Скучно в терминальной степени. Всё одно и то же, ничего нового.       Графоний феерически скуп и однообразен, как в плане детализованности иллюстраций, так и в плане использованной палитры цветов. Такой же отсутствующий уровень проработанности иллюстраций был в «Песне Сайи», но «Песнь» выпущена в третьем году, а «Купидон» — в шестнадцатом.        А ведь сценарий сам по себе достойный. И жути жуткие, и вертикальный инцест по обоим направлениям, и тотальный семейный деспотизм, и мистика, и раздвоение личности, и потребность в любви — автор годно продумала и увязала композицию, выбивающихся из последовательности элементов нет. Но цифровое воплощение истории получилось не годящееся никуда. И жути жуткие совершенно не развёрнуты.       Короче, не рекоминдую такие ВН.

[h1] “A Long Time Ago, in a Galaxy Far, Far Away…” [/h1]  A war rages between The Republic and The Sith. ‘Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic’ throws you head first into a fantastic recreation of the Star Wars universe filled with lightsabers, Sith Lords, and political intrigue, in an immersive, gripping tale of Good vs. Evil which - more than a decade on - stands tall as one of the best RPG’s of its generation, and probably the finest gaming interpretation of the iconic Star Wars franchise.  [b][u]Campaign:[/u][/b] Released in 2003 by Bioware | Lucas Arts, and set 4000 years before the events in ‘Star War’s - Episode 1: The Phantom Menace’, ‘SW:KOTOR’ tells the tale of a relative unknown caught up in events of cosmic proportions. The opening credits thrust you into the midst of an inter-galactic battle between Republic forces and a Dark Sith Lord, which finds you crash landing onto an alien planet, trying to stay alive and escape an inter-planetary Sith blockade. An unusually strong connection with the Force catapults the player from by-stander to protagonist, as an engaging, story-fueled campaign takes you across the galaxy from the mysterious water-world of Manaan, to the desert planet of Tatooine among many others. A lovingly crafted universe is filled with lots of recognizable faces to include – the treacherous Hutt’s, Bounty Hunter’s, Sith, Jedi Knights, Wookies, Protocol Droids, Rancor’s, and Sand People - amongst a broader cast of nearly 300 distinctive alien races.  [b][u]Gameplay | Graphics | Sound:[/u][/b] A Third-Person RPG in the classic mold, gameplay in ‘SW:KOTOR’ is built around the 4 pillars of ‘Character Development and Customization’, ‘Inventory Management’, ‘Combat’, and ‘Dialogue-driven Story-Telling’. You choose to play as one of three character classes (Soldier, Scout or Scoundrel – with both male and female options available), and then as one of three Jedi sub-classes (Sentinel, Consular or Guardian). A deep inventory system allows you to customize and equip your character with a multitude of clothing, weapon and armor options as well as assign XP to level-up in a variety of areas from Attributes, Skills, Feats, and Force Powers. Combat is based around the ‘D20’ RPG rule-set popularized in ‘Dungeons and Dragons (D&D)’, and while round-based, players are able to queue up actions and run them simultaneously in real-time. Finally, Character interaction is via a dialogue menu that is rumored to contain over 2000 lines of text, clearly geared toward maximizing player choice across multiple playthrough’s. While the broad strokes are seemingly representative of standard RPG fare, three elements serve to distinguish this title from the rank and file – 1.  The ability to switch to | customize | play as any character in your group provides for great overall variety 2. The campaign is well-paced with ‘Third Person’ gameplay broken up by ‘Rail-shooting’, ‘Stealth’, ‘Racing’, and ‘Gambling’ mini-games and 3. Deep customization options, lots of side-quests and the sheer glee of roaming the Star Wars universe adds great replayability to this title. Sound Design is also particularly noteworthy, with voice-acting, sound effects and background score composition all top-shelf. Well optimized K&M controls round out a well polished title.  [b][u]Flaws:[/u][/b] There is little to gripe about here, and perhaps the game’s biggest ‘flaw’ is its dated graphics - which have not aged particularly well - but it’s a testament to the overall strength of this title that it remains not only playable, but immensely engaging, despite this. Other minor issues include somewhat repetitive combat, and some minor character pathfinding issues.  Overall, ‘Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic’ is an erstwhile classic from another time, rich in Star Wars lore, with a deep, engaging campaign, a fantastic background score, compelling combat mechanics, high replayability and filled with iconic characters, plot twists, and moral complexities. This is a title you could easily lose yourself in for 50-60 hours on a single-playthrough, and that’s even before player-choice dictates your ultimate path to the Light or Dark Side. Ah, Firewatch - where to begin?  Having since followed Firewatch's development on their blog, and since admiring Olly Moss's artwork, I was already very much look forward to playing playing the game.  I was stoked.  Then teaser trailers were unveiled, and more and more hype started to be generated, and I was left slightly unsure as to what to expect from the finished title.  As with film trailers nowadays, sometimes a whole two hour story can be given away in just a trailer.  It's safe to say that Firewatch leaves much to be enjoyed and discovered in time, and I think it will be a story that I go back to enjoy in years to come (or so I hope).  Of the newer games that I have played and enjoyed in recent years, few have left me with such a huge set of feelings as after completing Firewatch.   For the time invested (as many people have pointed out how comparably short it can be to complete) it gives a lot in return.    I would put it in similar places to 'Her', 'Lost in Translation', 'Norwegian Wood', and many other stories that leave you with an uncertainty, an almost overwhelming sense of sadness, and a huge craving to find out the answers to 'what if' and 'why' things begin and end as they do in life.  It's not going to be a game for everyone, but I'm almost certian that everyone can take something away from Firewatch.  For the sentimental farts like myself, well it's just gold.  I would whole heartedly recommend this, even if you enjoy it (as I have) in just one sitting.  Love love love x

Really enjoyed my time with this game, which wasn't a whole lot.   I would say don't expect a lot of content from this. You will spend most of your time in your 'Okomotive' land craft, oftentimes jumping out to remove barriers via a simple yet intuitive set of puzzles.    Management of the Okomitve is quite entertaining, yet easy enough that it lets you soak in the eery atmosphere of the games post-apocalyptic world. I would love to see a more expansive title from this developer utilising the Okomotive management mechanics and expanding on their clear ability to craft an eery and unique post-apocalyptic world.   8/10

It’s really quite remarkable how South Park creators Trey Parker and Matt Stone have slowly ramped up the shock value over the past 17 years to keep the show sharp. Whether they and developer Obsidian could pull off the same for a 14-hour game instead of a 22-minute show was never a sure thing. But there I was, shrunk down to Underpants Gnome-size, crawling up Mr. Slave’s orifices to retrieve a WMD, slicing through gobs of bodily fluids in turn-based JRPG combat and climbing up half-digested corn-on-the-cob as I went, laughing hysterically the whole way. I’m floored at how consistently funny it is, and at how well the outrageous comedy melds with the relatively simple gameplay to create not just an amazing South Park game, but an intelligent and witty satire of roleplaying mechanics.  As for the story, it’s a clever premise that allows The Stick of Truth to take place in a recognizable and painstakingly recreated South Park setting, but also brings in all the usual fantasy roleplaying tropes through the power of children’s imagination. It’s a trick used many times in the show, and it works great for the game, too. An epic LARPing session (as casually set up by last year’s “Black Friday” trilogy of episodes) has your custom-created new kid in town joining either Cartman’s Humans or Kyle’s Elves, all dressed in amusingly bad makeshift cosplay outfits. True to the show, things escalate wildly and hilariously, leading to conspiracies involving the government, aliens, and Taco Bell.  Though it manifests itself in typically over-the-top South Park-ian ways, The Stick of Truth is a Paper Mario-esque RPG-lite. You and your single extra party member (you’ll unlock several South Park regulars, though only one can fight with you at a time) take turns battling formations of enemies, be it the Gingers, crazy homeless guys, aliens, and more. Typical buffs and debuffs are ably skinned in screwed-up fourth grader verbiage (throwing feces to add “gross out” effects) mixed with mana-powered spells and timed button-press attacks and blocks to keep you on your toes during combat. It keeps things simple enough while still leaving room for some tactical depth. And Obsidian refreshingly leaves out time-sink annoyances like character encumbrance and random battles you can’t avoid.  I couldn’t resist the curious lure of playing as the Jew class over the archetypal Fighter, Thief, and Mage options, but the differences between them turned out to be disappointingly slight. Sure, each has their own special abilities, but there are effectively no class-specific weapons or items, and there’s nothing to stop a Mage from choosing melee-enhancing gear and carving up foes with a blade just as well as a Fighter. All classes eventually learn special farting magic (a crude parody of Skyrim’s Dragon Shouts) though both the thumbstick motions and especially the tutorial sessions for your powers of flatulence tend to be cumbersome. Achievement or Trophy hunting aside, this lack of class differentiation or significant choices in the story are big reasons why I don’t feel much incentive to replay the campaign.  The other unfortunate offense is that some extremely useful things are poorly explained, if they’re even mentioned at all. Tricks like being able to switch your Buddy at any time by pressing down on the D-pad to access the Party menu, or taking the first swing at overworld enemies so that you get the first turn when the battle starts, and what your Buddies can do and are specifically good at are all up to us to discover accidentally. One other puzzling issue is the slipperiness of the action-selection wheel during combat – it’s strangely difficult to get your pointer to stick on the option you want, particularly if it’s in a diagonal slot on the wheel.  But that’s about the extent of the damage. Aesthetically, The Stick of Truth might be the most beautiful crappy-looking-on-purpose game I’ve ever seen. While it may seem trivial to make a role-playing game resemble the crude, construction-paper cutout style of the show, it’s executed so well here that the two mediums are almost indistinguishable. You’ll never see a HUD when walking around town, for instance, unless you tap the Y/Triangle button. Only the very rare stuck animation on an overworld enemy and (on both consoles, but not a capable PC) the occasional frame rate stutter when a new area loaded in for the first time reminded me that this was a game and not the show. And that was the extent of the technical problems I encountered.  Speaking of the quiet Colorado mountain town, it is itself one of the stars of The Stick of Truth. For the first time in the series’ history, it has been fully mapped out and given official geographical context. As a superfan who’s seen every episode of the show, I spent the first two to three hours of Stick of Truth exploring every kid’s house and each recognizable location, and from Stan’s bedroom closet (be sure to check it!) to Stark’s Pond and South Park Elementary, they’re all packed incredibly densely with in-jokes. Even every piece of inventory junk loot I collected is a show reference with a funny description attached to it.  A convenient fast-travel system eases post-exploration navigation, but various quests provide plenty of enticing reasons to comb the town throughout the adventure. Classic songs like “Taco-Flavored Kisses” and “Kyle’s Mom is a B****” are deployed with deft comedic subtlety on radios and in shops, and you absolutely must listen carefully for the particularly perfect use of Bigger, Longer, & Uncut’s “Blame Canada.”  The roughly 14 hours of absurdity and satire feels just right, from beginning to end. That being said, despite featuring over 100 characters and countless references, I wanted more. Towelie only ever shows up in a loading screen. Ditto the Talking Taco That Craps Ice Cream. The always-hilarious Christmas Critters have a criminally short cameo that is literally off-the-beaten-path. And while I’m being picky, I was also hoping for some sort of interactive or customized version of the show’s opening-credits Primus song that never came (though, laudably, any time you load up your save file, the instantly recognizable back-from-commercial-break guitar riff plays).  The Verdict  The Stick of Truth makes one thing abundantly clear: I never want to play another South Park video game made without Trey Parker and Matt Stone's direct, intimate involvement. With a controller in your hand, you are almost literally – gloriously – playing a 14-hour episode of South Park. There’s much, much more here for series fans than the uninitiated, but it’s a light but good quality role-playing game in its own right. It is, in a way, Season 18 all by itself. It is funny, shocking, self-effacing, and pretty much everything I could ask for from a South Park game -- even if it’s mostly a one-and-done experience.  9.0  + Feels like the show + Light but fun RPG system + Legitimately funny + Canada. The story is told through various comic strips, Max's internal monologues and surreal nightmares.  The only two bad things about the game? If you are a fan of Ridley Scott's Alien franchise, you will love SBTF.  SBTF is incredibly fun (most of the time). The game revolves around following the objective of collecting datacores, saving civilians, disabling the reactor, escaping alive, and of course, killing xenomorphs.  The game is extremely high stress and sometimes downright terrifying. Power can go out at anytime, Xenos kill you incredibly quickly, and the general ambience of the game feels exactly like Alien in the best way possible. The game has randomly generated maps meaning it always feels a tad different. You have turrets, fences, and of course your own guns to defend you from the xenos but ultimately the odds are against you.  The multiplayer in this game is fun but not perfect. Exciting for the fact that there is player collision and friendly fire, meaning you must be extremely careful of positioning, of course its also just fun playing with friends. Nothing better than mowing down waves of xenos with your buds. There is one small drawback as of right now, its a bit bugged at times. The game does not perform will under poor connectivity, this is expected of most games but SBTF seems to react worse than others. Mega stuttering, visual bugs, and all sorts of questionable scenarios happen. It isn't common and seems to mostly involve the specator camera but it can still be a bit annoying.   Graphically its nothing impressive, but thats okay. The ambience and lighting make up for that 100%. Not to mention that because of the quality of the graphics, the game can run on a wide variety of systems. Though the stability can become questionable when tons of xenos are introduced.   Overall I highly recommend Space Beast Terror Fright, there is a lot to offer here for any Alien fan or any fan of co-op shooters. It may not be a game you play consistently over many months, but it will be something you visit on occasion for a good space marine experience.

It's honestly difficult to pick between recommending this game or not. I got it because it was on sale, and I have fond memories of the SNES Final Fantasy games. I didn't know much about it going in, aside from that it has eight protagonists, and draws inspiration from FF6.  The Good:  - The game has a very strong combat system; a lot of older style JRPGs are simplistic and/or have a huge number of completely useless abilities. This game requires some thought, and the vast majority of abilities have their uses.  - This game can be surprisingly challenging for its genre; under normal circumstances I find that I can kind of mow over most encounters and bosses in most JRPGs, particularly older SNES/PS1-style games, but that's definitely not the case here. There's also some great use of late-game bosses messing with the game's interface, leading to some very memorable fights.  - Once you get past the first chapters, the Job system opens up and you can customize your party a  lot. Each character has a base class, and can have a second class at the same time, opening up stat bonuses and abilities from both. Plus, passive skills from any job you've unlocked can be equipped at any time. This gives a lot of options, without piling the characters down with dozens of abilities at once or feeling too overwhelming.  - The localization team took a lot of liberties with this game's script, and how certain characters speak, which can be a divisive decision. Overall, however, it's well-written, and the majority of the characters are likeable. Plus the game isn't part of some huge narrative like Trails, and the plot isn't particularly complex, so taking a bunch of liberties doesn't matter too much.  - The game has a unique visual style, and a great soundtrack.  The Bad:  - The eight characters have completely individual stories that don't even acknowledge the existence of the rest of the party, and in fact some of the narratives would break if the characters weren't alone. The only interactions between them take the form of Tales Of-style skits that you can activate between scenes. The stories barely connect with each other as well, outside of some very late-game content. They don't even feel thematically linked; it's almost like they established a setting, and had separate writers work on each character's story. This is made worse by the fact that by level scaling, you'll likely want to do each character's chapter 1, then each character's chapter 2, and so on. This wrecks the pacing since you'll leave off at some tense moment (particular in chapter 3s), then it will be some time later before you pick up that story again.  - While the individual character's chapters are generally well-written and interesting, the actual structure is very lazy. You will almost always arrive in a town, see some scenes, need to go along a trail with random encounters to a dungeon, and then explore a one screen dungeon with a bunch of branching paths with treasure chests. There's very little interesting treasure, as well, that exceeds what you can buy (or steal) in town, so it's not very exciting to find it. Sometimes the game mixes it up by putting the dungeon inside the town. Or having TWO screens for the dungeon. Amazing.  Overall: If you like classic JRPG style combat, you'll probably like this game. I do, so I recommend it. If you're looking for a deep story, however, you're not going to find it here and will likely be disappointed. Even if you like some of the characters' plots, there's too little content for each of them. I really wish they just made this a more traditionally structured game, with these same characters, in this same setting. From the limited interactions we do get, there's some strong dynamics they have with each other. Kind of disappointing this is the direction they went.

The short version.  Although a clone of Sid Meier's Alpha Centauri, Pandora is *not* Alpha Centauri. It is not even close. The art assets are far inferior, the diplomatic dialogs display the wit of a high-school student, and the factions, although almost identical to those of Alpha Centauri, are not motivated by their ideology, rather they display no obvious motivation at all. Indeed, they are often completely erratic, and will go to war for no reason, offer peace after losing a few units and then declare war again a few turns later. Over and over, and regardless of faction. They will also erratically make and break treaties over and over, and will throw snide comments at you in an attempt to sway the other factions against you. Independently of faction as well as over and over and over. Lastly, the quotes associated with the research lack the cultural sophistication of those from Alpha Centauri, and are often uninteresting or even annoying. In other words, the interest in the technologies and in the interaction between factions has been tossed out, and replaced with snide and ham-handed commentary.  Pandora changes the game situation a bit. Rather than mind-worms and a nascent god consciousness, Pandora has varied and aggressive indigenous lifeforms that have a significant role in player development as they will harass your early colonies and inhibit expansion. There is also another alien race that will pop in with superior technology and try to terraform the place as well as wipe everyone out more directly.  There are some improvements to the interface, the management system doesn't lock you in a modal update sequence after each turn, and you actually get incident reports that you can click on to find out what happened. So, to the author's credit, some improvement has been made, although you will still get multiple dialogs overlaying combat so they have failed to fully understand the concept of 'communication' and the difference between noise and information. On top of that there is the stack of making or breaking treaty dialogs and the personal carping communications after each turn ... well, maybe after every *second* turn.  Nevertheless, Pandora is a playable and a technically competent game on the Alpha Centauri model. If you thought that Alpha Centauri took itself too seriously and needed to lighten up, Pandora might work for you.

Com gráficos surpreendentes e quests que vão te fornecer intermináveis horas de jogatina, The Witcher 3 com certeza merece todos os prêmios e elogios que você encontrar por aí. Destaco também que, hoje, acredito que a CD PROJEKT RED é uma das únicas empresas que realmente se importa com seus consumidores e quer que os jogadores tenham a melhor experiência possível com seus jogos.   Se você, assim como eu, não gostava da jogabilidade da série nos games anteriores e achava inviável jogar, saiba que todo o gameplay foi reformulado e oferece um novo modelo de jogo - muito diferente de The Witcher e The Witcher 2. Dê uma chance ao terceiro game da série, valerá a pena.   PROS: - Gráfico - Arte - OST - Jogabilidade - Muitas horas de jogo - Grande número de side quests - Exploração: Há sempre alguma coisa nova para se descobrir nos mapas do jogo - História: Você pode ficar um pouco perdido se não acompanha a série, mas nada que torne-a uma experiência ruim  CONTRAS: É difícil citar contras de um jogo tão espetacular, mas vamos fazer um esforço. - Bugs: Até o momento não encontrei bugs que tornem o jogo inviável, mas é possível deparar-se com alguns bugs menores.  - Jogabilidade: No começo, pode ser beeem complicado de entender como funciona o combate e se acostumar com ele, é preciso algumas horinhas de jogo para se familiarizar com o sistema. Mas acredite, depois que descobrir como melhor aplicar as formulas e itens, além de aprender a desfrutar do combate, o jogo se tornará sensacional. - Ao passo que as telas de loading fazem um resumo do seu progresso no jogo e isso é muito legal nas primeiras horas, logo elas se tornarão chatas e repetitivas demais.
